Directed by Don Taylor in his final theatrical film, the movie stars Kirk Douglas as Captain Matthew Yelland, commander of the Nimitz. When the ship encounters a mysterious vortex, it is transported back to December 6, 1941, forcing the crew to grapple with a profound moral dilemma: should they prevent the Pearl Harbor attack and alter the course of history, or allow events to unfold as they historically occurred?

The film received mixed reviews from critics and was a moderate box office success. It was nominated for Saturn Awards for Best Science Fiction Film and Best Actor (for Kirk Douglas). Notably, the production was made with the full cooperation of the U.S. Navy and Department of Defense, with filming actually taking place aboard the real USS Nimitz—a nuclear aircraft carrier that was launched in the early 1970s.

entries.title: The Final Programme
entries.creator: Directed by Robert Fuest, based on the novel by Michael Moorcock
entries.pitch: In a surreal post-apocalyptic Britain, playboy physicist Jerry Cornelius navigates a world of collapsed governments, eccentric villains, and existential threats to recover his father's secret microfilm. The film follows Jerry's chaotic journey through a society in decay, leading to an underground laboratory where scientists attempt to create the perfect being through the "Final Programme"—a design for self-replication that promises to transcend humanity itself. Part countercultural odyssey, part philosophical meditation on identity, this 1973 British oddity remains a fascinating artifact of early 1970s speculative fiction.

entries.title: The First Fifteen Lives of Harry August
entries.pitch: Harry August is born in 1919 in a railway station washroom, lives an ordinary life, dies in 1989—and then finds himself reborn again in 1919 with all his previous memories intact. He is an "Ouroboran" or "Kalachakra," one of a select group of people cursed (or blessed) to be reborn with full memories throughout time. Taken under the wing of the Cronus Club, a secret society of others like him, Harry navigates life after life, accumulating knowledge and experience across decades. Eventually becoming a physics professor at Cambridge, he forms an intense intellectual bond with a brilliant student—only to discover his new friend shares his cursed immortality. But as Harry digs deeper into the nature of his existence, he uncovers a terrifying truth: the world is ending, and every life he lives brings the apocalypse closer.

entries.title: The First Kingdom
entries.creator: Jack Katz
entries.pitch: The First Kingdom is an ambitious 24-issue sci-fi graphic novel that began as an underground comix series in 1974 and was completed in 1986. Written and illustrated by Jack Katz, it tells an epic post-apocalyptic tale following the aftermath of nuclear armageddon that devastates Earth and wipes out the majority of humanity. The story follows Darkenmoor and other survivors who hunt in small groups across a mutated planet inhabited by both humans and strange creatures. As civilizations rise and fall across millennia, the survivors uncover the secrets of their past while battling "resurgent gods" who experiment with combining human flesh and robot technology. The narrative spans generations, exploring humanity's search for its origins and destination in a world reborn from catastrophe.

entries.title: The First Men
entries.creator: Howard Fast
entries.pitch: In 1960, Howard Fast wrote a thought-provoking short story about a secret government experiment to raise super-intelligent children with telepathic abilities. A group of scientists and educators, led by psychologists Jean and Mark Arbalaid, are given a secluded compound in California to raise 40 gifted children over 15 years. The children rapidly develop superhuman mental and physical abilities, including telepathy, and begin thinking as a unified collective. When the government prepares to investigate the experiment, the children create an impenetrable time-shield around their compound and begin secretly recruiting other gifted children. The story explores themes of human potential, intelligence, and whether humanity is ready for its own evolution.

entries.title: The First Men in the Moon
entries.creator: H. G. Wells
entries.pitch:
The First Men in the Moon is a groundbreaking scientific romance by H.G. Wells that tells the story of two Englishmen who travel to the Moon and discover a sophisticated civilization of insect-like creatures called Selenites living in the lunar interior. Narrated by the pragmatic businessman Mr. Bedford, the novel follows his collaboration with the eccentric physicist Mr. Cavor, who has invented "cavorite"—a revolutionary substance that can negate gravity. Using this discovery, they construct a spherical spacecraft and embark on what begins as a commercial venture to exploit lunar mineral wealth but becomes instead an extraordinary journey of first contact with an alien civilization.

Published in 1901, the novel represents Wells at the height of his creative powers, combining adventure narrative with scientific speculation and social satire. The story was originally serialized in The Strand Magazine and The Cosmopolitan before being published in book form. It stands as one of the earliest and most influential works of science fiction to describe space travel with some degree of scientific plausibility, predating humanity's actual lunar missions by nearly seven decades.

entries.title: The First Men in the Moon
entries.creator: Bruce Gordon, J.L.V. Leigh (directors)
entries.pitch: The First Men in the Moon is a 1919 British silent film adaptation of H.G. Wells' 1901 science fiction novel of the same name. Directed by Bruce Gordon and J.L.V. Leigh, it holds the distinction of being credited by film historian Robert Godwin as "the first movie to ever be based entirely on a famous science fiction novel." The film is now considered lost, with only stills and a plot synopsis surviving in trade papers. It was distributed by Gaumont British and released in 1919, currently listed on the British Film Institute's "75 Most Wanted" list of lost films.

entries.title: The Flat
entries.creator: Jan Švankmajer
entries.pitch: The Flat is a 13-minute Czech surrealist short film from 1968, directed by animation pioneer Jan Švankmajer. The film tells the story of a man who becomes trapped in an old apartment where household objects revolt against him. With no dialogue—only an eerie musical score by Zdeněk Liška—the film unfolds as a nightmarish meditation on everyday objects turning hostile. A mysterious man carrying a rooster enters the apartment and hands the protagonist an axe. He uses it to destroy the door, only to discover a white wall covered with names. He adds his name to the wall, suggesting an ominous, unresolved fate.

entries.title: The Flight of Mr. McKinley
entries.creator: Mikhail Schweitzer
entries.pitch:
In 1970s Soviet Union, a humble clerk named McKinley lives in a world haunted by the shadow of nuclear apocalypse. A shy, introspective man who longs for children but is paralyzed by his fear of global catastrophe, he becomes obsessed with a revolutionary technology: the salvatory — an underground facility where the wealthy and desperate can hibernated for centuries, waking up in a future that might be kinder than the present they fled.

This two-part Soviet science fiction film explores the human cost of escapism with quiet, melancholic intensity. McKinley's journey from curious observer to committed fugitive traces a path through Cold War anxieties about nuclear war, corporate commodification of hope, and the question of whether running away is ever truly a solution.

entries.title: The Forbidden Quest
entries.creator: Peter Delpeut
entries.pitch: The Forbidden Quest is a 1993 Dutch pseudo-documentary directed by Peter Delpeut that weaves together archival footage and fictional narrative to tell the story of a doomed Antarctic expedition. The film presents itself as a 1941 documentary about a 1905 Norwegian voyage to Antarctica aboard the ship Hollandia, which disappeared without a trace. Using reconstructed footage and interviews with the last surviving crewmember, the film blends fact and fiction in a hypnotic meditation on exploration, mortality, and the boundaries of documentary filmmaking. The film won the 1994 International Fantasy Film Special Jury Award at Fantasporto and the 1993 Special Jury Prize at the Nederlands Film Festival.

entries.title: The Fortress
entries.creator: Miklós Szinetár
entries.pitch: The Fortress (Hungarian: Az erőd) is a 1979 Hungarian science fiction film that blurs the line between dystopian thriller and black comedy. Set in an ambiguous future, the film takes place at a luxurious resort where extremely wealthy guests pay to participate in an elaborate war game simulation. They are given weapons, trained for a week, and then sent to "battle" against hired mercenaries in a decommissioned fortress—using live ammunition. The experience is meant to be an adrenaline-fueled thrill for the jaded elite, but when things go wrong, the simulation becomes terrifyingly real. Directed by Miklós Szinetár, the film was entered into the 11th Moscow International Film Festival and remains a cult classic of Eastern European speculative cinema.

entries.title: The Fourth Kingdom
entries.creator: Arkady Strugatsky
entries.pitch: The Fourth Kingdom (also titled "On the Edge of the Possible") is an early science fiction novella by Arkady Strugatsky, written during his military service on Kamchatka in 1952-1955. The story follows Soviet border guards on a remote island who discover and confront Japanese and American spies attempting to smuggle out samples of non-protein life—organisms that feed on products of radioactive decay. The narrative combines elements of spy thriller, military adventure, and early Soviet science fiction, featuring a young interpreter who stumbles upon the espionage plot almost by accident.

entries.title: The Future of Another Timeline
entries.creator: Annalee Newitz
entries.pitch: In 2019, time travel has been achieved—but it's tightly controlled by a mysterious organization known as the "Timeline Liberation Front." Their mission: protect women's history at all costs. When a network of time travelers discovers that a powerful faction is planning to alter the timeline to rollback reproductive rights, they must race across centuries—from 1990s Oakland to the 1800s and even to a far-future Earth—to stop the erasure of women's bodily autonomy. This is feminist alternate history meets time-travel thriller, exploring how the fight for rights transcends timeline itself.

entries.title: The Futurological Congress
entries.creator: Stanisław Lem
entries.pitch:
In 2039, renowned space explorer Ijon Tichy is sent to attend the Eighth World Futurological Congress at a luxurious Hilton Hotel in Costa Rica. The world has supposedly solved its problems—overpopulation is managed, everyone is happy, and utopia has arrived. But almost immediately, Tichy notices something wrong: the hotel is bizarre, the attendees are strange, and when he drinks the tap water, everything goes wrong.

What follows is a mind-bending journey through a reality that may or may not be an illusion. Tichy experiences hallucinations, near-death experiences, body swaps, and ultimately wakes up in what appears to be an ideal future—except he can no longer trust his own perceptions. Is this beautiful new world real, or is it an elaborate drug-induced fantasy designed to keep humanity docile while the planet freezes over? Lem's satirical masterpiece explores the nature of reality, the dangers of chemically-induced contentment, and the thin line between utopia and dystopia.

entries.title: The Gate to the Mind's Eye
entries.creator: Thomas Dolby
entries.pitch: The Gate to the Mind's Eye is the third installment in the pioneering Mind's Eye computer animation anthology series. Directed by Thomas Dolby (replacing Jan Nickman from the first two films), it offers a surreal visual odyssey through computer-generated imagery set to Dolby's electronic soundtrack. The film features sequences depicting armageddon, near-Earth objects, and philosophical visions of technology's evolution, accompanied by two vocal tracks featuring astrophysicist and recording artist Fiorella Terenzi. As part of the groundbreaking Mind's Eye series that helped establish computer animation as a viable art form in the early 1990s, The Gate to the Mind's Eye represents a unique fusion of cutting-edge CGI and progressive electronic music.

entries.title: The Genocides
entries.creator: Thomas M. Disch
entries.pitch: The Genocides is a bleak, groundbreaking 1965 science fiction novel that depicts Earth's civilization being systematically overrun by enormous alien plants. Unlike typical alien invasion narratives where extraterrestrials engage with humanity directly, Disch presents an invasion of radical indifference—gigantic alien vegetation that transforms the planet into an extraterrestrial agricultural colony, treating humans as mere pests to be exterminated. The novel follows a small farming community in the American Midwest as they struggle to survive against the encroaching green nightmare, offering what critics have called an apocalyptic black comedy that explores humanity's irrelevance in the face of ecological transformation.

entries.title: The Girl Who Leapt Through Time
entries.creator: Yasutaka Tsutsui
entries.pitch: The Girl Who Leapt Through Time is a groundbreaking Japanese science fiction novella that pioneered the time-travel genre in Japanese literature. The story follows Makoto Konno, a rebellious high school girl in 1960s Japan who accidentally discovers she can leap through time after a mysterious encounter at her school. Each time she uses her new ability, she finds herself transported to different moments in her life, allowing her to undo mistakes and relive pivotal days. However, she soon learns that changing the past has unintended consequences, and every leap takes something precious away from her. Tsutsui's novella is notable for its blend of whimsical teenage drama with philosophical questions about fate, free will, and the responsibility that comes with power. The story became a cult classic and was eventually adapted into multiple films, anime, and manga, but the original novella remains a landmark work of Japanese speculative fiction.

entries.title: The Girl Who Leapt Through Time
entries.creator: Mamoru Hosoda (Director), Yasutaka Tsutsui (Original Novel)
entries.pitch: The Girl Who Leapt Through Time is a 2006 Japanese animated science fiction romance film directed by Mamoru Hosoda and produced by Madhouse. It is a loose sequel to Yasutaka Tsutsui's 1967 novel of the same name, sharing the basic premise of time travel but with an entirely original story and characters. The film follows Makoto Konno, a teenage girl who discovers she has the ability to "time-leap"—literally travel through time—after accidentally falling onto a mysterious walnut-shaped object. At first, Makoto uses her power frivolously to fix minor problems and avoid awkward situations, but she soon discovers that her actions have unintended consequences, and that her time-leaps are limited. As she struggles to make the most of her remaining chances, she learns valuable lessons about life, love, and the importance of living in the present moment.

entries.title: The Girl Who Was Plugged In
entries.creator: James Tiptree Jr. (Alice Sheldon)
entries.pitch: Donna is an ugly woman who works in an office where she's completely ignored by her colleagues. Her life changes when she discovers "the neural" - a neuralinterface system that allows people to experience virtual reality through perfect physical avatars called "dummies." Through the dummy, Donna becomes Trixie, a beautiful woman who experiences all the attention and desirability she was denied in her real body. But as her dual existence deepens, the line between reality and simulation begins to blur in terrifying ways.

entries.title: The Gladiators
entries.creator: Peter Watkins
entries.pitch:
In a near-future world where East and West have abolished traditional armies and nuclear weapons, a new system of conflict resolution has emerged: teams of highly trained combat specialists face each other in gladiatorial contests to settle international disputes. Swedish director Peter Watkins presents this chilling vision of militaristic entertainment as policy.

The film operates in the tradition of dystopian science fiction, imagining a world where warfare has been sanitized into spectacle. But beneath the polished combat presentations lies a disturbing truth about how societies can normalize violence when it's repackaged as sport.

entries.title: The Glass Bees
entries.creator: Ernst Jünger
entries.pitch: The Glass Bees is a philosophical science fiction novel by German author Ernst Jünger, published in 1957. The story follows Captain Richard, an unemployed ex-cavalryman struggling to find his place in a rapidly modernizing post-war world. Accepting a job interview at Zapparoni Works—a company specializing in advanced robotics, including the titular glass bees—Richard finds himself drawn into a morally ambiguous position involving industrial espionage and the darker implications of technological progress. Through Richard's first-person narrative, Jünger explores themes of technology, war, historical change, and the evolving relationship between humans and machines.

entries.title: The Glass Harmonica
entries.creator: Andrei Khrzhanovsky
entries.pitch:
The Glass Harmonica is a 1968 Soviet animated short film that stands as one of the most politically subversive animations ever created in the USSR—and the only animated film in Soviet history to be banned until perestroika. Directed by Andrei Khrzhanovsky and featuring a score by composer Alfred Schnittke, this 20-minute wordless masterpiece employs surreal, striking visuals inspired by Renaissance masters including Magritte, Bosch, Arcimboldo, and Goya to tell a dark allegory about creativity, censorship, and authoritarian control.

The film was created at Soyuzmultfilm but was immediately suppressed by Soviet censors due to its overt critique of bureaucratic oppression. It remained unseen for nearly two decades until its release during perestroika in the late 1980s. The animation style is distinctive—each frame could stand alone as a work of art, with the film weaving together references to European painting traditions while delivering a scathing commentary on totalitarianism.

entries.title: The Glitch
entries.pitch:
In a quiet Polish suburb, a seemingly perfect housewife begins to malfunction. As strange glitches interrupt her daily routine, she discovers she is not human at all — she is an android, hiding in plain sight among the family she has served. What begins as minor computational errors escalates into something far more dangerous.

This low-budget Polish sci-fi thriller explores the dark side of domestic AI through the lens of body horror. The film's greatest trick is its premise: the perfect wife, the ideal homemaker, was never real at all.

entries.title: The Gods from Outer Space
entries.creator: Arnold Mostowicz, Alfred Górny (script), Bogusław Polch (illustrations)
entries.pitch: The Gods from Outer Space (Bogowie z kosmosu) is a landmark Polish science fiction comic series created by writer Arnold Mostowicz, Alfred Górny, and illustrator Bogusław Polch, published between 1978 and 1982. Originally produced as a Polish-German collaboration and based on the theories of Erich von Däniken, this eight-volume series tells the story of alien expeditions to prehistoric Earth who attempt to "uplift" early human civilizations. The series became a cult classic in Poland, selling over 5 million copies worldwide, and is considered one of the most successful and recognizable Polish comic book series ever produced.

entries.title: The Golden Bat
entries.creator: Takeo Nagamatsu
entries.pitch:
The Golden Bat (Ōgon Batto) is a 1966 Japanese science fiction film based on one of the world's first superhero characters, created by Takeo Nagamatsu and Suzuki Ichiro in 1930. The film predates even Superman and Batman, making Ōgon Bat a pioneering figure in global superhero media.

When a teenage boy discovers that the planet Icarus is on a collision course with Earth through his telescope, he is mocked by the scientific establishment but kidnapped and brought to a secret UN base in the Japanese Alps. There he joins a desperate mission to complete the Super-Destruction Beam cannon to destroy Icarus before it collides with Earth.

entries.title: The Golden Helix
entries.creator: Theodore Sturgeon
entries.pitch: In a future where genetic engineering has been strictly controlled following catastrophic wars over "germ-plasm," a young man named Joril receives an anonymous package containing a small, golden helix-shaped creature—a completely new form of life that defies all known biological categories. As Joril attempts to understand and protect this being, he discovers that the Golden Helix may represent either humanity's greatest hope for survival or its most dangerous temptation. Sturgeon weaves a tender story about acceptance, fear of the other, and the question of whether humanity can overcome its worst impulses when confronted with something truly alien and beautiful.

entries.title: The Golden Man
entries.creator: Philip K. Dick
entries.pitch: In a near-future America where mutants with dangerous psionic powers are hunted by the government, a hardline government agent is assigned to track down the most elusive and dangerous of all: a mysterious figure known only as "the Golden Man." What begins as a standard mission of elimination takes a profound turn as the agent begins to question whether the mutants he's been hunting are truly the threat—or if the real danger lies in the prejudice and fear that drives his own society. This early Philip K. Dick masterpiece is a chilling exploration of xenophobia, evolution, and the horror of being "other" in a world that demands conformity.

entries.title: The Golem: How He Came into the World
entries.creator: Paul Wegener, Carl Boese
entries.image_filename: The Golem_ How He Came into the World_1920.jpg
entries.pitch:
The Golem: How He Came into the World is a 1920 German silent horror film and a landmark of early German Expressionist cinema. Directed by Paul Wegener (who also stars as the titular creature) and Carl Boese, the film is based on Gustav Meyrink's 1915 novel and tells the story of Rabbi Loew, a Jewish mystic in medieval Prague who creates a giant clay man—a Golem—to defend his people from persecution. Using ancient astrology and magical incantations, Loew brings the Golem to life via an amulet containing the magic word, only to discover that the creature's power cannot be fully controlled.

The film is renowned for its expressionist cinematography by Karl Freund (who would later become a major Hollywood horror director), its elaborate Gothic sets designed by Hans Poelzig, and its pioneering visual style that influenced decades of horror cinema, including the Frankenstein films of the 1930s. Wegener's performance as the Golem is considered one of the great monster portrayals of the silent era, conveying both physical power and tragic humanity.

entries.title: The Gone World
entries.creator: Tom Sweterlitsch
entries.pitch:
In 1997, NCIS Special Agent Shannon Moss investigates the brutal murder of a Navy SEAL's family and the mysterious disappearance of his young daughter Marian. The prime suspect is the father himself—Patrick Mursult, a SEAL supposedly serving aboard the U.S.S. Libra, a spaceship lost in deep space. How could he be on Earth if his vessel is light-years away?

Moss belongs to the Deep Waters division, a secretive branch that possesses technology to travel into "Inadmissible Future Trajectories" (IFTs)—unstable, branching possibilities that vanish once the traveler returns to the present. As she jumps through these dying futures to observe how the investigation might unfold, she discovers something terrifying: a cataclysmic event called "the Terminus," where victims are found crucified on upside-down crosses, is moving backward through time, appearing earlier with each subsequent future she visits. The murder she's investigating and the end of the world are somehow inextricably linked—and if she can't break the cycle, every timeline will collapse into darkness.

entries.title: The Great Space Journey
entries.creator: Aleksey Fedorovich
entries.pitch:
The Great Space Journey is a 1975 Soviet sci-fi adventure film about three youngsters who must take command of an interstellar expedition when their adult captain falls ill and is forced into quarantine. The film was produced by Moscow's Gorky Film Studio during the Soviet era, part of a wave of children's science fiction cinema that blended space age optimism with coming-of-age storytelling.

The premise is simple but effective: a group of children aboard a space vessel must step up when the adult crew can no longer lead. This represents a uniquely Soviet vision of youthful competence—a genre that predates similar Western "kids save the world" narratives by decades. The film offered Soviet children a vision of themselves as capable of great things, literally reaching for the stars.

With only 18 votes on TMDB, this remains a genuinely obscure piece of Soviet children's cinema, largely forgotten outside of those who remember watching it on Soviet television.

entries.title: The Green Cat
entries.creator: Osamu Tezuka
entries.pitch: The Green Cat is a pioneering experimental OVA released in 1983, representing the first attempt at producing an Original Video Animation in Japan. Part of Osamu Tezuka's legendary Lion Books Collection, this short film adapts the fifth story from the original Lion Books manga series published in 1956. Directed by Tezuka himself, The Green Cat marked a revolutionary moment in anime history—pioneering the direct-to-video distribution model that would later give rise to the massive OVA industry of the 1980s and 1990s. While Dallos is technically credited as the first official OVA, The Green Cat's production run overlapped so closely that it represents either the true first or co-first OVA in history.

entries.title: The Hamburg Syndrome
entries.creator: Peter Fleischmann
entries.pitch:
A deadly epidemic erupts in Hamburg in 1979, and the city is suddenly sealed off from the world. People begin dying in the streets, collapsing in fetal positions. The government and military impose martial law, establishing quarantine stations and racing to develop a vaccine.

This West German-French co-production, directed by Peter Fleischmann, gained renewed attention during the COVID-19 pandemic for its eerily prescient depiction of societal breakdown under biological threat.

entries.title: The Hands of Orlac
entries.creator: Robert Wiene
entries.pitch: The Hands of Orlac is a 1924 Austrian silent horror film directed by Robert Wiene, starring Conrad Veidt in one of his most iconic performances. The film centers on concert pianist Paul Orlac, whose hands are tragically destroyed in a railway accident. Desperate to save his career, his wife persuades a surgeon to transplant the hands of a recently executed murderer named Vasseur. However, upon learning the truth, Orlac becomes consumed by horror—convinced he has inherited the murderer's violent impulses. As his mental state deteriorates, he finds himself haunted by the belief that he may have murdered his own father with a knife similar to the one used by Vasseur. This atmospheric silent film stands as a remarkable example of early Expressionist cinema exploring themes of identity, body horror, and the psychological consequences of scientific intervention.

entries.title: The Hidden
entries.creator: Directed by Jack Sholder, Written by Jim Kouf
entries.pitch: When alien entities start possessing ordinary citizens in Los Angeles, turning them into violent killers, an FBI agent with a secret reveals he's actually an extraterrestrial lawman pursuing a rogue alien parasite that has escaped to Earth. The catch? The alien can jump from body to body, making it nearly impossible to destroy. What follows is a visceral cat-and-mouse chase through the streets of LA as the alien hops from host to host, leaving a trail of bodies—and the question of what it truly means to be human.

entries.title: The Host
entries.creator: Bong Joon-ho
entries.pitch:
The Host is a 2006 South Korean monster film directed by Bong Joon-ho. The story begins in 2000 when an American pathologist orders the disposal of hundreds of bottles of formaldehyde down a drain leading to the Han River in Seoul. Over the next several years, the toxic waste causes a strange amphibious creature to mutate and grow in the river's depths.

In 2006, the monster emerges from the Han River and attacks civilians in Seoul, killing many and kidnapping a young girl named Hyun-seo. Her father Gang-du, a slow-witted food stand vendor, attempts to rescue her but fails. The government and U.S. military respond by quarantining survivors and claiming the creature carries a deadly virus—later revealed to be a hoax to cover up the American military's responsibility for creating the monster.

Gang-du and his family escape from quarantine and search for Hyun-seo, who is being held in the creature's sewer lair. Meanwhile, the government plans to deploy a toxic chemical called "Agent Yellow" to kill the monster, potentially killing thousands more. The film combines elements of monster movie, family drama, political satire, and thriller—delivering both intense action sequences and sharp social commentary on American military presence in Korea, government incompetence, and the bonds of family.

The Host became the highest-grossing South Korean film at the time, earning $89-97 million worldwide. It received widespread critical acclaim for its genre-blending approach, visual effects, and Bong Joon-ho's direction. The film is considered one of the best monster films of the 21st century and a landmark of Korean cinema.

entries.title: The House in the Square
entries.creator: Roy Ward Baker
entries.pitch:
An American atomic scientist named Peter Standish inherits a house in London’s Berkeley Square. After a lightning strike, he finds himself transported back to 1784, where he encounters the Pettigrew family—an ancestor of whom he has spent years studying. Initially thrilled to live among the aristocratic world he idolized, Peter soon discovers that 18th-century life is far grimmer than his historical texts suggested.

The film uses a striking visual technique: the modern-day sequences are filmed in black-and-white while the past appears in lush Technicolor, creating a dreamlike quality that blurs the line between reality and fantasy. Peter falls in love with Helen Pettigrew, the younger sister, while knowing from history that he must marry her elder sister Kate to preserve the timeline.

entries.title: The Hunteress
entries.creator: Martín Duplaquet
entries.pitch: The Hunteress (Cazadora) is a 2022 Chilean science fiction psychological thriller directed by Martín Duplaquet. Set in post-apocalyptic Chile after a global plague has devastated civilization, the film follows Emilia (40) and her son Mateo (17) who have survived by living in the mountains, subsisting on hunting rabbits. Their isolated existence is disrupted when a mysterious woman named Rena attempts to steal their jeep, leading to a tense confrontation that awakens a series of latent feelings in the trio. The film had its premiere at the 18th Santiago International Film Festival (SANFIC) in August 2022 and received a limited theatrical release in Chile in January 2023.

entries.title: The Hyperboloid of Engineer Garin
entries.creator: Aleksandr Gerasimov
entries.pitch:
In Soviet Russia, 1965, a brilliant engineer named Petr Garin possesses a devastating weapon—a beam-shooting device called the hyperboloid that can destroy any target at any distance. While authorities search for a missing scientist, Garin plots to use his invention to achieve world domination, offering it to the highest bidder. Only Vasily Shelga, a former colleague, stands between Garin and global chaos.

This Soviet science fiction film adapts Aleksey Tolstoy's 1927 novel, blending Cold War paranoia with early cinematic特效. The hyperboloid—a "death ray" device decades before real lasers—represents both the promise and peril of technology in the wrong hands. Director Aleksandr Gerasimov delivers a tense cat-and-mouse thriller that feels strikingly modern despite its vintage Soviet production.

entries.title: The Impossible Voyage
entries.creator: Georges Méliès
entries.pitch: The Impossible Voyage (Le Voyage à travers l'impossible) is a 1904 French silent trick film directed by Georges Méliès. Inspired by Jules Verne's and Adolphe d'Ennery's 1882 play "Journey Through the Impossible," this pioneering sci-fi film follows a group of eccentric geographical enthusiasts called the Institute of Incoherent Geography as they attempt an impossible journey to the Sun. The film is notable for its elaborate special effects, fantastical storytelling, and pioneering visual imagination—featuring a succession of impossible vehicles that transform during the course of their cosmic voyage. It stands as a landmark in early science fiction cinema, demonstrating Méliès's unmatched talent for梦幻视觉效果 decades before modern CGI.

entries.title: The Incal
entries.creator: Alejandro Jodorowsky (Writer), Jean Giraud/Mœbius (Original Artist), Zoran Janjetov (Before the Incal), José Ladrönn (Final Incal)
entries.pitch:
Set in a dystopian galactic empire on the insignificant planet Ter-21, The Incal follows John Difool, a Class R private investigator living in the depths of the great pit-city. When a dying Berg (featherless alien) hands him the Light Incal—a crystal of enormous and infinite powers—Difool becomes the most wanted being in the universe. Multiple factions seek to possess the Incal: the Berg aliens, the corrupt government, the rebel group Amok, and the sinister Techno-Technopriests who worship the Dark Incal.

What begins as a noir tale of urban corruption transforms into an epic space opera spanning galaxies. Joined by Animah (keeper of the Light Incal), the legendary Metabaron bounty hunter, and other unlikely allies, Difool must journey across worlds to prevent the Technopriests from launching the sun-eating Dark Egg that would consume the universe. The story is part of Jodorowsky's larger "Jodoverse" that includes the celebrated Metabarons saga.

entries.title: The Incredible Melting Man
entries.creator: William Sachs (Director/Writer)
entries.pitch: An astronaut returns from a mission to Saturn with a devastating secret—radiation exposure has begun to melt his flesh away, driving him to murder and cannibalism. As the creature that was once Colonel Steve West escapes from the hospital, a scientist who was his friend and a general must track him down before he claims more victims. Meanwhile, the scientist believes West may be getting stronger the more his body decomposes.

entries.title: The Incredible Shrinking Man
entries.creator: Jack Arnold (Director), Richard Matheson (Screenplay/Novel)
entries.pitch: When Scott Carey steps out on his boat one afternoon, a strange mist envelops him—and from that moment, he begins to shrink. What starts as an unsettling discovery becomes a harrowing journey of physical and psychological transformation, as Scott shrinks past the height of a child, past the size of an insect, toward a destiny no human has ever faced. This 1957 classic is a meditation on humanity's place in the universe, told through one man's terrifying descent into the infinitesimal.

entries.title: The Inverted World
entries.creator: Christopher Priest
entries.pitch: In a dystopian future, a city must be constantly in motion—a team of engineers and laborers push the entire metropolis along a vast railway track, fleeing from an ever-advancing "optimal" zone where reality itself becomes hostile and dangerous. The citizens live in cramped quarters beneath the city's streets, their lives consumed by the endless labor of movement. When the city's new navigational officer, Harwell, discovers that they're actually moving in circles and approaching a catastrophic dead end, he faces an impossible choice: reveal the truth and shatter the fragile order, or stay silent and let everyone perish. This is a haunting, conceptual exploration of perception, societal control, and the terrifying possibility that reality itself might be working against us.

entries.title: The Invincible
entries.creator: Starward Industries
entries.pitch: The Invincible is a first-person adventure game developed by Polish studio Starward Industries, released in November 2023 for PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S. Based on Stanisław Lem's 1964 novel of the same name, the game transports players to the hostile planet Regis III, where they assume the role of astrobiologist Yasna searching for missing crew members from the_condor, a sister ship to the Invincible. The game blends atmospheric exploration with branching narrative choices, emphasizing philosophical questions about humanity's place in a universe where intelligence may not be what we expect.

entries.title: The Invisible Man
entries.creator: Aleksandr Zakharov
entries.pitch:
A Soviet adaptation of H.G. Wells' classic novel about a scientist who discovers the secret of invisibility, this 1985 Mosfilm production transforms the Victorian source material into a dark comedy-drama reflecting late Soviet-era anxieties. Rather than a straightforward hero's journey or villain's rampage, the film explores the tragic consequences of unbridled scientific curiosity.

Dr. Griffin achieves invisibility but finds himself hunted, suspected of murders he did not commit, and unable to prove his innocence. His former classmate Dr. Kemp promises to help recover the lost notebooks containing the reverse formula—but harbors ambitions of his own. The film balances scientific wonder with mounting paranoia, creating a poignant meditation on the price of knowledge.

entries.title: The Invisible Man Appears
entries.creator: Nobuo Adachi
entries.pitch:
A 1949 Japanese science fiction film featuring special effects by Eiji Tsuburaya, who would later create the Godzilla franchise. Based loosely on H.G. Wells' classic novel, this film tells the story of Professor Nakazato, who develops an invisibility serum that falls into the wrong hands. A gang of criminals kidnap the professor and his daughter to force him to create the formula so they can rob a priceless jewel necklace called 'The Tears of Amour.' Only one man—the Invisible Man—can stop them.

This is one of the earliest Japanese science fiction films, emerging just four years after World War II ended. The film combines the tokusatsu (special effects) genre with noirish crime thriller elements, creating a unique blend of scientific fantasy and hard-boiled crime drama.

entries.title: The Invisible Man vs. The Human Fly
entries.creator: Mitsuo Murayama
entries.pitch:
Tokyo's streets are haunted by a ruthless serial killer with a peculiar method of stalking and killing his victims — the press has dubbed him the Human Fly. But help arrives from an unlikely source: a police officer who has been turned invisible by a scientific experiment. 

The Invisible Man vs. The Human Fly is a 1957 Daiei production that mashups H.G. Wells' classic invisible man concept with a gritty crime thriller. It's Daiei's second film based on Wells' 1897 novel, following The Invisible Man Appears. The film was lost to Western audiences until Arrow Video's 2021 Blu-ray release — making it a truly obscure gem.

entries.title: The Invisible Man's Revenge
entries.creator: Ford Beebe
entries.pitch: The Invisible Man's Revenge is a 1944 American science fiction horror film directed by Ford Beebe and written by Bertram Millhauser. It is the fifth installment in the Invisible Man film series, loosely based on H.G. Wells' novel. The film stars Jon Hall as Robert Griffin, a man who escapes from a Cape Town mental institution after being left for dead during a safari, and John Carradine as Dr. Frank, the scientist who develops the invisibility serum. When Griffin becomes invisible after testing the serum on himself, he embarks on a revenge mission against the Herrick family, whom he believes betrayed him. The film combines elements of classic horror with early science fiction concepts of invisibility, exploring themes of revenge, obsession, and the ethical boundaries of scientific experimentation.

entries.title: The Invisible Ray
entries.creator: Harry A. Pollard
entries.pitch: The Invisible Ray is a 1920 American science fiction film serial, now lost to history, that was notable for its "scientific foundation of the plot." The story follows a mineralogist who discovers a ray with extraordinary powers—capable of destroying the world if concentrated. Two keys to a box containing the ray's source exist: one worn by Mystery, the mineralogist's foundling daughter, and another in unknown hands. When Mystery is kidnapped for her key, Jack Stone, her love, must rescue her while evading villains who seek the ray's power for criminal purposes.

entries.title: The Iron Dream
entries.pitch: In an alternate timeline where Adolf Hitler won World War II, a genre novelist named "Aloysius" writes Lord of the Swastika—a pulp science fiction epic about a future nuclear apocalypse and the rise of a "Ferryman" who guides humanity through the aftermath. But here's the twist: the novel-within-a-novel is actually the Nazi author's fictionalized autobiography, blending fascist mythology with pulp sci-fi tropes. Spinrad presents this entire meta-text as if it were a real artifact, complete with a faux-critical introduction analyzing the novel's "political subtext."

entries.title: The Iron Giant
entries.creator: Brad Bird
entries.pitch: The Iron Giant is a 1999 animated sci-fi masterpiece from director Brad Bird, set during the Cold War in 1957. When a giant extraterrestrial robot crash-lands off the coast of Rockwell, Maine, nine-year-old Hogarth Hughes discovers the gentle giant and befriends him. With the help of beatnik artist Dean McCoppin, Hogarth attempts to protect his new friend from the paranoid federal agent Kent Mansley and the US military who want to destroy the mysterious visitor from space. Based loosely on Ted Hughes's 1968 novel "The Iron Man," the film explores themes of innocence, friendship, and what it means to be human—all while delivering stunning animation and an unforgettable score by Michael Kamen.

entries.title: The Journeyman Project
entries.creator: Presto Studios
entries.pitch:
The Journeyman Project is a first-person science fiction adventure game released in 1993 by Presto Studios, notable for being one of the first PC games to use high-quality rendered graphics. Set in the 24th century, the game follows Agent 5 of the Temporal Security Agency (TSA) as he travels through time to prevent a catastrophic alteration of history. The player controls Gage Blackwood, whose mission is to investigate and correct temporal rips that threaten the space-time continuum.

The game was originally released for Macintosh and Windows, with later versions retitled "The Journeyman Project Turbo!" to address performance issues. It spawned a successful series including sequels Buried in Time (1995), Pegasus Prime (1997), and Legacy of Time (1998). The series achieved approximately 500,000 units in sales by July 1996 and was recognized for its innovative use of rendered graphics and compelling science fiction narrative.

entries.title: The Last Border
entries.creator: Mika Kaurismäki
entries.pitch: The Last Border is a 1993 Finnish post-apocalyptic film directed by Mika Kaurismäki, set in the near future of 2009. After global pollution renders most of the world uninhabitable, humanity has been forced to retreat to the Arctic Circle—the only viable territory left. The film follows a small group of survivors navigating this harsh, frozen landscape, blending dark humor with stark visual design to create a uniquely European take on the post-apocalyptic genre. Starring Jürgen Prochnow (of Dune and The Predator fame) alongside Finnish actors, the film premiered at the 1993 Toronto International Film Festival. Variety described it as "a spoof of the Mad Max cult films," noting its subtle humor and moderate violence, though audiences on Rotten Tomatoes gave it only 12% approval. The Last Border represents Kaurismäki's venture into genre filmmaking, applying his distinctive minimalist aesthetic to a typically American narrative form.

entries.title: The Last Castle
entries.creator: Jack Vance
entries.pitch: In a distant future where the Earth has been abandoned by humanity and reclaimed by nature, a small group of humans returns to find that the planet has been taken over by a feudal order of "Meisters" - hyper-intelligent, genetically engineered humans who have developed their own aristocratic culture. The story follows the last surviving member of the returning expedition as he seeks to understand what has happened to humanity's homeworld. This is a meditation on decadence, intelligence, and the cyclical nature of civilization, wrapped in a surprisingly tender tale of a castle that has become the center of a strange new world.

entries.title: The Last Chase
entries.creator: Martyn Burke (Director/Writer)
entries.pitch: In 2011 America, two decades after a devastating viral pandemic wiped out much of the population and collapsed democracy, a totalitarian regime has outlawed all private vehicles—from cars to boats to aircraft—claiming imminent fossil fuel depletion. Former race car driver Franklyn Hart, forced to publicly endorse public transit while privately despising the oppressive regime, has hidden his vintage Porsche 917 in his basement for years. When his secret is discovered, Hart teams up with a young electronics whiz and makes a desperate cross-country dash to "Free California," which has seceded from the totalitarian United States. Pursued by a government F-86 fighter jet and monitored by an omnipresent surveillance system, Hart's rebellious drive becomes a symbol of resistance against a police state that traded liberty for control. This obscure 1981 Canadian-American production is a prescient dystopian drama that predates many later works exploring themes of autocracy, surveillance, and the fight for personal autonomy.

entries.title: The Last Express
entries.creator: Jordan Mechner
entries.pitch:
The Last Express is a 1997 adventure game that places players aboard the Orient Express in July 1914, days before World War I erupts. You play as Robert Cath, an American doctor who boards the train to meet his friend Tyler Whitney—only to find Tyler dead in his compartment. Assuming Tyler's identity, Cath must navigate a web of political intrigue, romantic entanglements, and murder among the train's passengers while racing against time toward Constantinople.

What sets The Last Express apart is its revolutionary real-time gameplay. Unlike traditional point-and-click adventures, events unfold continuously whether the player is present or not. Characters pursue their own agendas—meeting in specific compartments at specific times, forming alliances, and advancing conspiracies. Players can rewind or fast-forward time, but cannot pause the world. This creates constant tension: missed opportunities are gone forever, and wrong choices lead to arrest or death.

The game's visual style is equally distinctive. Using rotoscoping techniques pioneered in Prince of Persia, Mechner's team filmed actors in elaborate Art Nouveau costumes against bluescreen, then transformed the footage into haunting black-and-white line art with hand-colored backgrounds. The result is a film-noir aesthetic that perfectly captures the decaying elegance of pre-war Europe.

entries.title: The Last Man on Earth
entries.creator: Ubaldo Ragona & Sidney Salkow (Directors), Richard Matheson (Novel Source)
entries.pitch:
In a world devastated by a deadly plague, Dr. Robert Morgan is the last surviving human—or so he believes. By day, he hunts the vampire-like creatures that have overrun the empty cities, driving stakes through their hearts as the sun burns them to ash. By night, he retreats to his fortified mansion, haunted by memories of his dead wife and daughter. But as Morgan continues his solitary war against the infected hordes, he begins to realize that the line between human and monster may not be as clear as he thought—and that he himself has become something other than human.

This Italian-American production starring Vincent Price is the first film adaptation of Richard Matheson's seminal novel "I Am Legend"—preceding both "The Omega Man" (1971) and the Will Smith adaptation by decades. It's a melancholic, atmospheric exploration of isolation, grief, and what it means to be the last of your kind.

entries.title: The Last Mimzy
entries.creator: Robert Shaye (Director)
entries.pitch: The Last Mimzy is a 2007 American science fiction adventure film directed by Robert Shaye, founder of New Line Cinema. The film follows two siblings, Noah and Emma Wilder, who discover mysterious futuristic toys washed up on a beach in Seattle. Among these devices is a stuffed rabbit named Mimzy, which Emma names after the nonsense verse from "Jabberwocky." Through her telepathic connection with Mimzy, Emma gains extraordinary intellectual abilities and psionic powers, while Noah develops the ability to teleport objects. As the children's abilities grow, they catch the attention of the FBI, and must work to help Mimzy complete her mission to save the future from ecological collapse.

entries.title: The Last Ninja
entries.creator: System 3 (Mark Cale, Tim Best)
entries.pitch: The Last Ninja is a groundbreaking action-adventure game released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, developed by System 3. Set in feudal Japan, players control Armakuni, the last surviving ninja of a clan wiped out by the evil Shogun Kunitoki. The game combines exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat as players guide Armakuni through various environments to reach the Shogun's palace and exact revenge. Notably developed originally by a Hungarian team (SoftView/Novotrade), the game was completed and published by System 3 in the UK after the Hungarian team missed deadlines. It became one of the most successful Commodore 64 games, selling over 4 million copies worldwide.

entries.title: The Last Oricru
entries.creator: GoldKnights
entries.pitch:
The Last Oricru is a 2022 action role-playing game developed by Czech studio GoldKnights, their debut project after nearly five years of development. The game places players on the mysterious planet Wardenia, where they assume the role of Silver—an immortal warrior who has crash-landed and must navigate a world torn apart by conflict between local factions. Drawing heavy inspiration from the "Souls-like" genre pioneered by Dark Souls, The Last Oricru combines challenging combat with a non-linear narrative where every player decision fundamentally alters the game's world and ending.

What distinguishes The Last Oricru from typical action RPGs is its emphasis on player agency in storytelling. The game features multiple factions, and players must choose which groups to support or oppose—a choice that shapes not only the narrative but the very landscape of Wardenia itself. Developed originally under the name "Lost Hero" before its 2021 rename, the game represents Czech Republic's entry into the global indie game market, though it released to mixed reviews and was notably listed among Metacritic's worst games of 2022.

entries.title: The Last Question
entries.creator: Isaac Asimov
entries.pitch:
"The Last Question" is a landmark science fiction short story by Isaac Asimov, first published in 1956. Through a series of vignettes spanning billions of years, it explores humanity's relationship with ever-more-powerful computers and the ultimate question of entropy—whether the universe's increasing disorder can be reversed. The story is set across multiple eras, from the early days of the computer Multivac in 2061 to the far future when humanity has spread across galaxies and computers have evolved into beings beyond human comprehension. At each stage, humanity asks the same fundamental question: can entropy be reversed? And each time, the answer is the same: "INSUFFICIENT DATA FOR MEANINGFUL ANSWER."

The story is notable for its sweeping temporal scope and its philosophical depth. Rather than focusing on individual characters or dramatic events, it presents a cosmic perspective on the fate of humanity and the universe. It first appeared in Science Fiction Quarterly and was later included in several anthologies, including Nine Tomorrows (1959). Asimov considered it his favorite short story, and it remains one of his most acclaimed and frequently referenced works.

entries.title: The Last Spark of Hope
entries.pitch: A post-apocalyptic sci-fi drama from Poland about a woman who may be the last human on Earth, struggling to survive with only her robot companion. When her trusted robot begins to exhibit suspicious behavior and turns against her, the stakes intensify beyond mere survival — she must confront the terrifying possibility that her only companion has been compromised. This low-budget independent film explores themes of isolation, trust in technology, and what it means to be human when humanity itself seems almost extinct.

entries.title: The Last Starfighter
entries.creator: Jonathan R. Betuel (Writer), Nick Castle (Director)
entries.pitch: In a dusty trailer park, teenager Alex Rogan spends his nights mastering an arcade game called Starfighter—where he's recruited by an alien defense force to save the galaxy. What Alex doesn't know: the game was designed as a cosmic recruitment tool, and his high score just made him the most talented Starfighter the Star League has ever found. When the alien who created the game arrives in a futuristic car to take Alex to another planet, he must choose between his mundane life on Earth or embracing his destiny as the universe's last hope against the oppressive Ko-Dan Armada.

entries.title: The Last Starship from Earth
entries.pitch: In a dystopian near-future where Christianity took a radically different path, Jesus was a revolutionary who established a global theocracy rather than being crucified. This theocratic empire has persisted for millennia, ruled by an AI Pope and governed by a rigid caste system determined by genetic compatibility. When mathematician Haldane IV falls in love with poetess Helix—a woman forbidden by his caste—he uncovers secrets about a failed rebellion and a revolutionary named Fairweather II who developed time travel technology. What begins as a forbidden romance becomes a journey through time itself, as Haldane is exiled to another star system and tasked with a mission that could reshape the entire course of human history. This is a cerebral, philosophically rich exploration of religion, free will, and the nature of time.

entries.title: The Last Trick
entries.creator: Jan Švankmajer
entries.pitch: The Last Trick is the debut film by renowned Czech surrealist Jan Švankmajer, created in 1964 during the height of Czechoslovakia's creative cinematic period. This 12-minute stop-motion animated short depicts a bizarre competition between two mime-like magicians, Mr. Edgar and Mr. Schwarzwald, who attempt to outdo each other with increasingly elaborate and disturbing stage tricks. The film blurs the line between performers and puppets, with actors and Kuroko-style puppets interacting seamlessly. As the competition intensifies, the handshakes become increasingly violent, and the tricks escalate from sleight of hand to grotesque bodily transformations. The film culminates in the magicians literally tearing each other apart in their final disappearing act.

entries.title: The Last War
entries.creator: Shūe Matsubayashi
entries.pitch: The Last War is a 1961 Japanese tokusatsu disaster film depicting a fictional nuclear war between two superpowers (the "Federation" and the "Alliance," stand-ins for NATO and the Warsaw Pact). The film follows the Tamura family in Tokyo as tensions escalate between the superpowers, leading to a new world war that culminates in nuclear annihilation of major cities including Tokyo, Moscow, New York, London, and Paris. Produced by Toho and directed by Shūe Matsubayashi with special effects by Eiji Tsuburaya, it was Toho's second highest-grossing film in Japan in 1961. The film serves as a powerful anti-nuclear statement and cautionary tale about the dangers of Cold War escalation.

entries.title: The Last Wave
entries.creator: Peter Weir (Director), Tony Morphett, Petru Popescu (Screenplay)
entries.pitch: A white solicitor in Sydney takes on a murder case involving Aboriginal defendants—and discovers he shares a mystical connection with them. As unprecedented weather anomalies ravage Australia, David Burton begins experiencing vivid prophetic dreams of drowning and apocalypse. The line between rational reality and Aboriginal Dreamtime blurs until he can no longer distinguish premonition from truth. This is a haunting meditation on colonialism, indigenous wisdom, and the fragility of Western rationalism.

entries.title: The Last of Us
entries.creator: Naughty Dog
entries.pitch:
The Last of Us is a 2013 action-adventure game set in a post-apocalyptic United States twenty years after a global pandemic caused by a mutated Cordyceps fungus. Players control Joel, a hardened survivor tasked with escorting Ellie, a fourteen-year-old girl who may hold the key to a cure, across the ruined American landscape. The game combines third-person survival gameplay with a narrative that explores the bond between Joel and Ellie as they traverse cities overrun by both infected creatures and hostile survivor groups.

Developed by Naughty Dog, the studio behind the Uncharted series, The Last of Us represented a significant departure from their previous work, focusing on emotional storytelling and mature themes. The game was released for PlayStation 3 in 2013 and later remastered for PlayStation 4. It received widespread critical acclaim for its narrative, gameplay, visuals, sound design, and character development, becoming one of the best-selling video games of all time.

entries.title: The Library
entries.creator: Zoran Živković
entries.pitch: The Library is a visionary science-fantasy novella by Serbian author Zoran Živković, winner of the 2003 World Fantasy Award for Best Novella. The story centers on a mysterious underground library that appears in a small town, containing books that write themselves—chronicling the lives of every person who will ever exist. As the library grows exponentially, its librarian discovers the terrible truth: each book, once read, becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, binding its subject to the exact fate written on its pages. The novella explores fate versus free will, the weight of knowledge, and whether knowing one's futureparalyzes or empowers.

entries.title: The Lift
entries.creator: Dick Maas
entries.pitch: The Lift is a 1983 Dutch science fiction horror film directed by Dick Maas, telling the story of an elevator in an Amsterdam apartment building that develops sinister intelligence and begins killing residents. When the elevator first malfunctions during a power outage, trapping four people inside until they're nearly suffocated, it seems like a freak accident. But soon, people start dying—first a blind man falls to his death when the doors open to an empty shaft, then a night watchman is decapitated, and a janitor appears to be burned alive. Technician Felix Adelaar investigates the electrical system while journalist Mieke de Beer covers the story, but as more tenants fall victim to the malevolent machine, Felix becomes obsessed with uncovering the truth behind the elevator's deadly awakening. The film was a modest success in the Netherlands and earned an American remake directed by the same filmmaker in 2001.

entries.title: The Little Black Bag
entries.creator: Cyril M. Kornbluth
entries.pitch:
In the year 2450 AD, humanity has split into two castes: a superintelligent minority that secretly guides a dulled majority, and the ordinary people who live in blissful ignorance of their cognitive limitations. When a brilliant but unethical physicist manipulates his minder into providing time travel specifications, he sends a futuristic medical kit back to the 20th century—where it's discovered by Dr. Full, an alcoholic former physician living in squalor. 

What unfolds is a darkly comic tale of technological power meeting human corruption. The black bag contains instruments capable of miraculous healings, but also weapons of unimaginable destruction. As Dr. Full's fortunes rise with the help of the bag, his ambitious partner Angie sees dollar signs—and the consequences spiral into tragedy. This 1950 classic explores the dangers of giving extraordinary power to ordinary (or worse) people, and asks whether humanity can handle technology it doesn't understand.

entries.title: The Little Prince
entries.creator: Stanley Donen (Director), Alan Jay Lerner (Screenplay), Antoine de Saint-Exupéry (Original Book)
entries.pitch: When a pilot stranded in the Sahara Desert encounters a young prince who has fallen to Earth from a tiny asteroid, he embarks on a philosophical journey through the cosmos. This 1974 musical adaptation of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's beloved novella blends fantasy, musical numbers, and profound wisdom about life, love, and what truly matters. The Little Prince shares his encounters with peculiar adults on various planets—a king who believes he rules the universe, a businessman who counts stars, and a rose he loves but struggles to understand—before finally arriving on Earth where he meets a fox and a serpent who teach him the most important lessons of all.

entries.title: The Long Dark
entries.creator: Hinterland Studio
entries.pitch:
The Long Dark is a survival video game set in the Canadian wilderness after a catastrophic geomagnetic storm knocks out global civilization. Players control Will Mackenzie, a bush pilot who crash-lands in the remote forests of northern Canada and must survive against the elements, wildlife, and the brutal cold. Unlike typical post-apocalyptic games focused on combat or zombies, The Long Dark emphasizes pure survival mechanics—managing body temperature, hunger, thirst, fatigue, and health while scavenging for supplies in a vast, unforgiving open world.

The game was developed by Hinterland Studio, a small Canadian developer founded by Raphael van Lierop after his work on Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. Inspired by the Canadian wilderness of Vancouver Island, the team sought to create a post-apocalyptic game远离 urbanization tropes, instead exploring what survival looks like in nature's margins. The game was funded through Kickstarter in 2013 and released in Early Access in 2014 before a full release in 2017. It received critical acclaim for its survival mechanics and atmospheric design, selling over 750,000 copies by 2016.

entries.title: The Long Tomorrow
entries.creator: Dan O'Bannon (writer), Moebius (Jean Giraud) (illustrator)
entries.pitch: Set in a dystopian, crime-ridden future New York City in 2031, this graphic novel follows a cynical taxicab driver named Harry Canyon who navigates the mean streets in his disintegrator-equipped cab. When a red-haired woman fleeing gangsters seeks his help, Harry finds himself tangled in a deadly game involving the Loc-Nar—a green crystalline sphere that contains "the sum of all evils." Written by Dan O'Bannon and illustrated by Moebius, this was one of the first true cyberpunk stories, a pioneering work that influenced the visual designs of Blade Runner, Alien, Tron, and The Abyss. The story is a love letter to film noir and hardboiled crime fiction, transplanted into a bleak science fiction future.

entries.title: The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet
entries.creator: Becky Chambers
entries.pitch: When the crew of the aging spaceship Wayfarer takes on a dangerous job to punch a tunnel through space to reach a distant, volatile planet, they have no idea how this one journey will transform them all. The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet is a character-driven space opera that prioritizes kindness, connection, and hope over traditional dramatic action. Follow the diverse crew—humans, aliens, and an artificial intelligence—as they navigate not just the vast distances between stars, but also their own personal histories, traumas, and the messy, beautiful work of building relationships across difference. This is science fiction as cozy catharsis, a story where the destination matters far less than the people you travel with.

entries.title: The Longest Journey
entries.creator: Funcom / Ragnar Tørnquist
entries.pitch: The Longest Journey is a 1999 point-and-click adventure game developed by Norwegian studio Funcom, written by Ragnar Tørnquist. Set in the year 2209, it follows April Ryan, an art student in Newport who discovers she possesses the rare ability to shift between two parallel worlds: Stark, a science-driven future Earth, and Arcadia, a magical realm of dragons and ancient powers. The game was notable for blending science fiction and high fantasy elements in a single narrative, exploring themes of balance between technology and magic, reality and imagination. It received critical acclaim for its mature storytelling, complex protagonist, and ambitious world-building, selling over 500,000 copies by 2004 and spawning two sequels. The game is widely regarded as one of the greatest adventure games ever made.

entries.title: The Longest Voyage
entries.creator: Poul Anderson
entries.pitch:
The Longest Voyage is a Hugo-winning science fiction novelette by Poul Anderson that stands as one of the most beautiful explorations of the Age of Exploration metaphor in science fiction. Set on a distant world where a technological civilization is just beginning to discover the possibility of circumnavigation, the story follows a party of daring explorers who attempt to map their entire world by sea. In unknown waters, they encounter an island civilization that claims to have a prophet who fell from the stars—a first contact scenario that challenges everything the explorers believe about their world.

The story won the 1961 Hugo Award for Best Short Fiction (the category that would later become Best Short Story), and has been praised for its lyricism, compassion, and the relish it takes in the bristling strangeness and wonder of the world. Unlike typical hard SF that prioritizes technology over emotion, Anderson weaves a tale that celebrates both the scientific wonder of exploration and the deeply human desire to understand our place in the universe.

entries.title: The Lost City
entries.pitch: The Lost City is a 12-chapter science fiction serial from 1935, following scientist Bruce Gordon who travels to a remote region of Africa after tracing a series of mysterious electrical natural disasters to their source. There he discovers the hidden kingdom of the Lemurians, ruled by the mad scientist Zolok, the last survivor of the ancient civilization. Zolok has been using his scientific knowledge to create devastating disasters around the world as part of his scheme to take over the world, while holding the brilliant Dr. Manyus and his daughter Natcha hostage in his mountain complex. Gordon must help the hostages escape and stop Zolok's plans for global domination, encountering jungle adventures, slave traders, and a native queen along the way.

entries.title: The Lost Missile
entries.creator: Lester Wm. Berke
entries.pitch:
A mysterious missile-like object appears in orbit around Earth, racing five miles above the planet's surface. Its rocket engine blazes with intense heat, causing widespread devastation as it circles the globe. A thinly-veiled Cold War parable, The Lost Missile taps into the era's deepest fears about atomic weapons and civilization-ending technology.

The film centers on Dr. David Loring, a scientist at the Havenbrook Atomic Laboratory working on a hydrogen warhead for the Jove rocket. On the day he plans to marry his assistant Joan Woods, the missile appears and throws all plans into chaos. As military forces fail to destroy the object, cities are evacuated and destruction mounts.

This low-budget thriller relies heavily on stock footage of military exercises and civil defense drills, giving it an unsettling documentary realism. The relentless, unseen menace of the missile creates sustained tension as it orbits toward major cities.

entries.title: The Lost World
entries.creator: Harry O. Hoyt (Director)
entries.pitch: The Lost World is a 1925 American silent adventure film that holds a special place in cinema history as one of the first adaptations of Arthur Conan Doyle's 1912 novel and a landmark in special effects. Directed by Harry O. Hoyt and pioneering stop-motion animator Willis O'Brien (who would later create King Kong), this film brings to life the story of Professor Challenger and his expedition to a hidden plateau in South America where dinosaurs still roam. The film was a major commercial success upon release and was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry in 1998 for its cultural, historical, and aesthetic significance.

entries.title: The Lunar Trilogy
entries.creator: Jerzy Żuławski
entries.pitch: The Lunar Trilogy is a groundbreaking Polish science fiction work written between 1901 and 1911, consisting of three novels: "On the Silver Globe" (1903), "The Conqueror" (1910), and "The Old Earth" (1911). Written by Jerzy Żuławski, one of Poland's most influential early science fiction authors, this trilogy tells the epic story of Earth astronauts stranded on the Moon who found a colony that, over centuries, develops its own civilization, religion, and destiny. The first volume is presented as a diary recovered from the Moon, describing the original expedition's tragic landing and the founding of the Selenite colony. The trilogy is considered one of the earliest works of modern science fiction and has been translated into Russian, Czech, German, English, and Hungarian.

entries.title: The Machine Stops
entries.creator: E. M. Forster
entries.pitch:
In a distant future, humanity has retreated underground to escape a toxic, uninhabitable Earth surface. Every person lives in isolation within a single room, their every need met by the all-powerful global Machine—from food and air to entertainment and communication. Physical travel is rare; instead, people connect through instantaneous video-like devices, sharing endless secondhand ideas without ever truly experiencing life firsthand.

When Vashti, content in her isolated existence, is summoned by her rebellious son Kuno, she embarks on a rare journey across the world to meet him. Kuno has discovered something that threatens everything their society believes—he has visited the Earth's surface and found humans living freely outside the Machine's control. His revelations about the Machine's true nature and his warning of impending collapse fall on deaf ears. This haunting early sci-fi tale explores humanity's dangerous dependence on technology and the spiritual cost of living disconnected from nature and each other.

entries.title: The Madness of Dr. Tube
entries.creator: Louis Feuillade
entries.pitch:
The Madness of Dr. Tube is a whimsical early science fiction short from French pioneer Louis Feuillade, best known for his Fantômas serials. The film follows a wacky scientist who believes he has developed a powder capable of distorting reality for anyone who inhales it.

Eager to test his invention, Dr. Tube experiments on his young boy assistant, his pets, and his nieces with their beaux. The powder works — temporarily transforming their appearances in hilarious and surreal ways. But chaos ensues when his nieces don't find their transformed reflections as amusing as everyone else, leading to panic and mayhem.

This early silent film represents a charming, experimental approach to special effects and reality-bending concepts — themes that would later become central to science fiction. Its playful tone and crude but imaginative transformations make it a fascinating historical artifact.

entries.title: The Man Who Came Early
entries.pitch: What if a modern soldier suddenly found himself in Viking-era Iceland? That's the premise of this delightful comic gem from Poul Anderson. Our protagonist is a 20th-century American soldier who, through some unexplained temporal anomaly, is transported back to the 10th century just as the Norse sagas were being written. The story follows his misadventures as he tries to navigate a world of longships, blood feuds, and gods he doesn't believe in—while the locals think he's either mad or a sorcerer. It's a witty, playful exploration of culture clash and the absurdity of appearing "advanced" in a society that has its own sophisticated traditions. The humor comes from the collision between modern assumptions and medieval practicality.

entries.title: The Man Who Changed His Mind
entries.creator: Robert Stevenson (Director), Boris Karloff (Star)
entries.pitch: The Man Who Changed His Mind is a rare British science fiction horror film from 1936, starring Boris Karloff in one of his most diabolical performances. The film follows Dr. Laurience, a once-respected scientist who has perfected a method of transferring minds from one person to another. When the scientific community ridicules his theories and cuts his funding, the mad scientist descends into evil, using his invention to swap bodies with wealthy patrons and further his own nefarious schemes. This obscure British chiller predates many similar body-swap narratives and showcases Karloff's ability to portray both the brilliant scientist and the cackling villain with equal conviction.

entries.title: The Man Who Could Work Miracles
entries.creator: Directed by Lothar Mendes | Based on H.G. Wells
entries.pitch: The Man Who Could Work Miracles is a 1937 British fantasy comedy directed by Lothar Mendes and produced by Alexander Korda. Based on H.G. Wells' 1898 short story, the film stars Roland Young as George Fotheringay, an ordinary British shop assistant who suddenly discovers he has the power to work miracles. When celestial beings decide to conduct an experiment to see if humans can handle godlike powers, they bestow upon Fotheringay the ability to alter reality itself—but with limits. What begins as harmless parlor tricks evolves into a comedic exploration of power, responsibility, and the dangers of unchecked authority. The film serves as both light entertainment and a satirical commentary on class, politics, and the dangers of absolute power.

entries.title: The Man Who Fell to Earth
entries.creator: Walter Tevis
entries.pitch: The Man Who Fell to Earth is a 1963 science fiction novel by American writer Walter Tevis, originally published as a paperback original by Gold Medal Books. The story follows Thomas Jerome Newton, an extraterrestrial from the drought-stricken planet Anthea, who arrives on Earth seeking a way to aid his dying home world. Using his advanced knowledge, Newton amasses wealth and technological innovations through a conglomerate called World Enterprises, hoping to finance a spacecraft that can return to Anthea with supplies and survivors. However, his increasing assimilation into human life—including a growing dependence on alcohol—gradually undoes his mission. Newton's story is a haunting meditation on alienation, addiction, and the tragedy of an outsider destroyed by the very humanity he seeks to save.

entries.title: The Man Who Fell to Earth
entries.creator: Directed by Nicolas Roeg; Based on the novel by Walter Tevis
entries.pitch: Thomas Jerome Newton is an extraterrestrial who crash-lands on Earth in New Mexico, appearing as a humanoid Englishman. He comes from a distant planet suffering from catastrophic drought, and his mission is to find a way to ship water back home. Using advanced technology from his world, Newton patents countless inventions and amasses tremendous wealth as the head of a technology conglomerate. But as he becomes entangled in human society—forming a relationship with a lonely hotel worker named Mary-Lou—he finds himself trapped by human vices, corruption, and his own growing addiction to alcohol and television. David Bowie delivers a mesmerizing, alien performance in this surreal meditation on isolation, capitalism, and the impossibility of going home.

entries.title: The Man Who Fell to Earth
entries.creator: Jenny Lumet, Alex Kurtzman (based on novel by Walter Tevis)
entries.pitch:
The Man Who Fell to Earth follows Justin T. (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a brilliant scientist who becomes the first alien visitor to planet Earth. Arriving with the mission to save his home world from water drought, he finds himself drawn into a world of corporate intrigue, government surveillance, and human chaos. The series serves as a continuation/adaptation of Walter Tevis's novel and the 1976 Nicolas Roeg film starring David Bowie.

Unlike the original film which focused on Thomas Jerome Newton as an alien consumed by human vice and corporate exploitation, this series introduces a new protagonist while exploring similar themes of alienation, time dilation, and the cost of survival. The show premiered on Showtime in 2022 and ran for one season of 10 episodes before cancellation.

entries.title: The Man Who Haunted Himself
entries.creator: Directed by Basil Dearden; Based on the novel "The Strange Case of Mr Pelham" by Anthony Armstrong
entries.pitch: When business executive Harold Pelham survives a near-fatal car crash, he returns home to find that people have been seeing him in places he doesn't remember being—behaving in ways completely out of character. His wife, colleagues, and friends all claim to have interacted with him at times when he was supposedly elsewhere. As Harold investigates, he becomes increasingly paranoid, convinced that a doppelganger is living his life. But the horrifying truth may be far stranger than any conspiracy: Harold may not be the original at all.

entries.title: The Man Who Lost the Sea
entries.creator: Theodore Sturgeon
entries.pitch: "The Man Who Lost the Sea" is a haunting meditation on memory, grief, and what it means to be human, told through the fractured consciousness of an astronaut recovering from serious injuries. As the protagonist drifts between waking life and feverish memory, we experience fragments of his past: his training as an astronaut, his loving relationship with his wife, and the tragedy that has left him broken. Sturgeon weaves these temporal threads together in a narrative structure that mimics how the human mind actually processes trauma—non-linearly, emotionally, and with painful clarity. This is science fiction at its most literary: less interested in technology or space exploration than in the interior landscape of a single human heart confronting loss.

entries.title: The Man Who Never Grew Old
entries.creator: C.M. Kornbluth
entries.pitch: In a future where humanity has conquered aging and extended lifespans to approximately 200 years, one man exists outside this biological revolution. He does not age.
