entries.title: UFO: Afterlight
entries.creator: Altar Games
entries.pitch: UFO: Afterlight is a 2007 real-time tactics and turn-based strategy video game developed by Altar Games, a Czech studio. It is the third installment in the UFO series, following UFO: Aftermath and UFO: Aftershock. Set on Mars, the game continues the story of human survival following the catastrophic alien invasion of Earth depicted in earlier titles. Players manage a colony of 10,000 humans in cryo-sleep, working to terraform the Red Planet while defending against emerging threats from ancient alien robotics and hostile extraterrestrial factions. The game received mixed reviews, holding a score of 71/100 on Metacritic.

entries.title: UFO: Aftermath
entries.creator: ALTAR Interactive
entries.pitch: UFO: Aftermath is a 2003 real-time tactics/turn-based strategy video game developed by Czech studio ALTAR Interactive. Set in a post-apocalyptic near-future, the game puts players in command of humanity's last remaining military force after alien spores devastate Earth. The title serves as a homage to the classic X-COM series, combining global strategic management with squad-based tactical combat missions. Players must rebuild civilization, research alien technology, and mount a defense against the alien threat that has already wiped out most of humanity.

entries.title: UFO: Enemy Unknown
entries.creator: Julian Gollop / Mythos Games / MicroProse
entries.pitch: UFO: Enemy Unknown (also known as X-COM: UFO Defense) is a groundbreaking turn-based strategy video game that defined the alien invasion genre in gaming. Released in 1994 by MicroProse, players take command of X-COM (Extraterrestrial Combat), a secret international organization tasked with defending Earth from alien invasions. The game combines tactical ground combat with resource management and research elements, creating a tense, strategic experience where every decision matters. Players must intercept UFOs, investigate crash sites, capture aliens for research, and develop new weapons and technology to face increasingly sophisticated extraterrestrial threats. The game's difficulty, depth, and atmosphere created a cult classic that influenced countless subsequent strategy and tactics games.

entries.title: Ulagam Sutrum Valiban
entries.creator: M.G. Ramachandran (Director)
entries.pitch:
Ulagam Sutrum Valiban (transl. "Globetrotting Youngster") is a 1973 Indian Tamil-language science fiction film directed and co-produced by M.G. Ramachandran, one of Tamil cinema's most iconic figures. The film follows Murugan, a brilliant Indian scientist who discovers a method to harness and store the energy from lightning using a revolutionary formula. At an international scientists' conference in Hong Kong, he demonstrates the destructive potential of his discovery—a single pellet-sized object can bring down trees and set surroundings ablaze—but refuses to share it with the world, fearing it will be used for destructive purposes amid rising Cold War tensions.

When a wealthy industrialist named Bairavan offers $100 million to sell the research to foreign "deep state" agents, Murugan refuses and pretends to burn his notes. He embarks on a world tour with his girlfriend Vimala, actually hiding the notes in a safe location. Pursued by Bairavan and his agents across Singapore, Bangkok, and Japan, Murugan must protect his groundbreaking discovery while navigating betrayal, amnesia-inducing weapons, and international intrigue. His younger brother Raju, a CBCID officer, joins the hunt to find him, leading to an action-packed climax at Expo '70 in Osaka.

entries.title: Ultraman Zearth
entries.creator: Tsuburaya Productions
entries.pitch:
Ultraman Zearth is a 1996 Japanese tokusatsu film that serves as a loving parody of the iconic Ultraman franchise. Released to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the original Ultraman, the film introduces a hero unlike any traditional Ultra warrior—a peculiar alien from the Land of Pikari in Nebula Z95 who has an obsessive fixation on cleanliness.

The hero's human identity is Katsuto Asahi, a young man who shares Zearth's peculiar aversion to dirt. What makes Ultraman Zearth truly unique is his transformation method: rather than dramatic poses or mystical devices, he transforms by using an electric toothbrush called the Pikari Brusher—a detail that perfectly encapsulates the film's comedic tone. His mission on Earth is to combat pollution and the monsters that threaten the planet, though his hygiene fixation often proves more troublesome than helpful.

The film strikes a careful balance between genuine tokusatsu action and self-aware humor, making it an ideal entry for fans of the Ultra series looking for something different. The parody extends beyond the hero to include send-ups of classic Ultraman tropes, characters from the original series appearing in comedic contexts, and a generally lighter take on the alien superhero formula.

entries.title: Undersea Kingdom
entries.creator: B. Reeves Eason, Joseph Kane (Directors)
entries.pitch: Undersea Kingdom is a 12-chapter Republic Pictures sci-fi serial released in 1936, created as a direct response to Universal's successful Flash Gordon. The story follows Lieutenant Crash Corrigan, a Navy officer, who joins Professor Norton and reporter Diana Compton on an expedition to investigate disturbances emanating from the legendary lost continent of Atlantis. Using Professor Norton's revolutionary rocket submarine, the team travels to the undersea city, only to discover it's caught in a civil war between the noble White Robes led by Sharad and the tyrannical Black Robes commanded by Unga Khan. Unga Khan possesses a devastating Disintegrator device capable of generating earthquakes, and he plans to use it to conquer Atlantis and then destroy the surface world. It's up to Crash and his allies to stop Unga Khan before he unleashes catastrophic destruction on civilization.

entries.title: Universal War One
entries.creator: Denis Bajram
entries.pitch: In the not-so-distant future, humanity has colonized the outer reaches of the solar system. But when a mysterious, incomprehensible black wall appears near Saturn—absorbing all light and matter and cutting off access to the outer planets—tensions between Earth and the colonization companies explode into all-out civil war. Enter the Purgatory Squadron: a band of soldiers given a second chance after courts-martial for crimes ranging from cowardice to rape. Led by the principled Captain June Williamson, this ragtag group of criminals and outcasts must investigate the black wall before the war destroys humanity's future among the stars.

entries.title: Uridium
entries.creator: Andrew Braybrook (designer), Graftgold (developer)
entries.pitch: Uridium is a horizontally scrolling shooter designed by Andrew Braybrook for the Commodore 64 and published by Hewson Consultants in 1986. The game challenges players to destroy fifteen Super-Dreadnoughts orbiting each planet in a galactic sector, each draining mineral resources from planetary cores. Players control a Manta class Space Fighter, navigating through enemy defenses, destroying surface installations, and landing on massive motherships to extract fuel rods before escaping as the Dreadnought explodes. The game is notable for its innovative parallax scrolling technique on the Commodore 64 and was a critical success, winning Best Shooting Game of 1986 and earning a Golden Joystick Award.

entries.title: Urusei Yatsura 2: Beautiful Dreamer
entries.pitch: In this 1984 animated film from director Mamoru Oshii, a group of high school students at Tomobiki prepare for their annual cultural festival—but reality itself begins to unravel. Ataru Moroboshi and his classmates experience time loops, discover their entire city exists on the back of a giant turtle in space, and encounter dream demons challenging their perceptions of what's real. This experimental anime blends surrealist imagery with philosophical questions about simulation, dreams, and existence, years before similar concepts appeared in Western films like Groundhog Day or Inception. Oshii's departure from the comedic tone of the original manga toward existential themes makes this a unique, thought-provoking entry in the anime canon.

entries.title: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders
entries.creator: Jaromil Jireš (director), based on novel by Vítězslav Nezval
entries.pitch: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders is a 1970 Czechoslovak Gothic surrealist dark fantasy film, considered one of the last and most haunting works of the Czechoslovak New Wave. Directed by Jaromil Jireš and based on Vítězslav Nezval's 1935 novel, the film follows 13-year-old Valerie as she navigates a disorienting dreamscape populated by vampires, priests, and mysterious strangers. Blending Gothic horror, eroticism, and surrealist imagery, the film presents a nightmarish coming-of-age story where reality and fantasy merge into something unsettling and hypnotic. The film's unique visual style, combining baroque set design with expressionist cinematography, has earned it cult status among fans of Eastern European fantasy and horror cinema.

entries.title: Vampires of Geona
entries.creator: Unknown
entries.pitch:
In this obscure 1991 Soviet sci-fi film, the GALAX Concern sends a crew to the distant planet Geona to harvest its valuable natural resources. But they're not alone on this hostile world — poisonous, pterodactyl-like creatures the locals call \"vampires\" defend their territory with deadly ferocity. Two crew members are already immobilized by vampire bites when Inspector Yanin arrives to assess the situation and lead the fight against the creatures.

The film blends creature horror with a corporate exploitation narrative, reflecting the anxieties of late-Soviet era cinema about Western corporate interests and the exploitation of natural resources. The \"vampire\" creatures are not supernatural monsters but evolved predators defending their ecosystem — a subtle ecological metaphor hidden within the creature feature framing.

With only 10 documented votes on TMDB, this is a genuinely obscure piece of Soviet sci-fi that rewards fans of low-budget creature features and those interested in the forgotten corners of Soviet genre cinema.

entries.title: Vesper
entries.creator: Kristina Buožytė, Bruno Samper (Directors)
entries.pitch: Vesper is a 2022 science fiction film directed by Lithuanian filmmaker Kristina Buožytė and French director Bruno Samper, marking their second collaboration following 2012's Vanishing Waves. Set in a bleak post-apocalyptic Earth, the film follows the eponymous Vesper, a resourceful 14-year-old girl who lives in a forest with her paralyzed father, communicating only through a drone that resembles a floating robot head. The film presents a world where humanity's attempt to prevent ecological collapse through genetic technology catastrophically failed—engineered viruses and organisms escaped into the wild, wiping out edible plants, animals, and large portions of the human population. Now, an oligarchic elite thrive in enclosed cities called "citadels," while the remaining survivors struggle outside, dependent on coded seeds traded by the citadels. The film premiered at the 2022 Karlovy Vary International Film Festival and was shot primarily outdoors in Vilnius, Lithuania, with a budget of €5 million.

entries.title: Viaje al planeta Júpiter
entries.creator: Segundo de Chomón
entries.pitch:
Viaje al planeta Júpiter (Le Voyage sur Jupiter / A Trip to Jupiter) is an 8-minute silent short film from 1909, directed by the pioneering Spanish filmmaker Segundo de Chomón. Produced by Pathé Frères in Paris, this early science fiction film is part of a wave of early 20th-century cinematic space exploration fantasies that followed in the wake of Georges Méliès' influential A Trip to the Moon (1902). The film depicts a fantasy journey from Earth to Jupiter, showcasing the technological optimism and curiosity about space travel that characterized the era's scientific imagination. Chomón, often called the "Spanish Méliès," was renowned for his innovative special effects and trick photography, and this film demonstrates his mastery of stop-motion animation and theatrical spectacle.

The film is notable for its place in cinematic history as one of the earliest depictions of interplanetary travel in European cinema, and for representing Spain's contribution to early science fiction filmmaking during the silent era. Its production came during a period of intense experimentation in filmmaking techniques, where directors like Chomón pushed the boundaries of what could be captured on film, creating fantastical visions of worlds beyond Earth that captivated early movie audiences.

entries.title: Visitors from the Arkana Galaxy
entries.creator: Dušan Vukotić
entries.pitch: Visitors from the Arkana Galaxy is a quirky Yugoslav-Czechoslovak science fiction comedy from 1981, directed by the acclaimed animator Dušan Vukotić. The film follows Robert, a hotel doorman who is obsessed with science fiction and dreams of writing his own SF novel about three alien androids from the advanced civilization of Arkana. To his astonishment, actual aliens from his imagination land on a nearby island one night, leading to a surreal series of events where fiction and reality blur dangerously. The film won awards at the Fantasporto festival and stands as a delightful example of Eastern European sci-fi comedy.

entries.title: Visitors from the Galaxy
entries.creator: Dušan Vukotić
entries.pitch: Visitors from the Galaxy (Gosti iz galaksije) is a wild Yugoslav-Czechoslovak sci-fi comedy from 1981, directed by the acclaimed animator Dušan Vukotić. The film follows Robert, an aspiring science fiction writer who discovers he has the unique ability to materialize his thoughts into reality. While working on his long-gestating novel about aliens, Robert accidentally brings the extraterrestrial characters from his imagination to life—including a female android named Andra, two space children, and a bizarre monster designed by the legendary surrealist animator Jan Švankmajer. What follows is a surreal, boundary-pushing tale that blends sitcom-style domestic comedy with increasingly absurd sci-fi mayhem, including nudity, decapitations, and psychedelic visual effects. The film is a quirky, genre-bending artifact from a vanished era—when Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, countries that no longer exist, collaborated on their own spin on Star Wars-era space comedy.

entries.title: Wahan Ke Log
entries.creator: N. A. Ansari (Director)
entries.pitch:
Wahan Ke Log (transl. "People from Out There") is a 1967 Indian Hindi-language science fiction film and one of the earliest sci-fi films produced in India. Directed by Nisar Ahmed Ansari and produced by Bundelkhand Films, the film stars Pradeep Kumar, Tanuja, and Johnny Walker. The story follows Agent Rakesh, who is assigned by the Chief of the Central Intelligence Service to investigate the mysterious murder of Dinanath in Karolbagh, with suspicion of alien involvement from Mars.

The film was made on a low budget and promoted with the tagline "The strange visitors from Mars are on the way." Despite its campy production values, it has drawn scholarly attention as one of the only science fiction pictures from India during that era. According to researcher Sami Ahmad Khan, the film seems to have taken inspiration from the Sino-Indian War that occurred five years prior, though no direct reference to China appears in the narrative. Contemporary reviews were critical, with Link magazine noting "Credibility is not by any means its forte," though later retrospectives have called it "an unusual film, an interesting blend of a ghost and thieving aliens."

entries.title: Waking Up Yesterday
entries.creator: Milan Šteindler
entries.pitch:
A Czech teacher discovers a way to journey into the past — specifically to the late 1980s — to recover his lost love Eliška. In the present (2012), Peter is a hopeless romantic who has failed at relationships, becoming a social laughing stock. But he knows that in 1988, everything was different: he and Eliška were together, happy, before circumstances drove them apart.

The film is a bittersweet romantic comedy wrapped in time travel mechanics, set against the backdrop of late Communist Czechoslovakia. Peter's radical opinions about the socialist system make him a target for the secret police, even though he technically »knows« from his future knowledge that the regime will collapse within a year.

What makes this film special is its dual nature: a personal quest for lost love that doubles as an inadvertent political commentary on a society that no longer exists.

entries.title: Wakusei Robo Danguard Ace
entries.creator: Leiji Matsumoto, Dan Kobayashi
entries.pitch:
Wakusei Robo Danguard Ace (Planetary Robot Danguard Ace) is a 56-episode Japanese anime television series created by the legendary Leiji Matsumoto—best known for Space Battleship Yamato and Galaxy Express 999—with Dan Kobayashi. Produced by Toei Animation and airing from March 1977 to March 1978, it was Matsumoto's sole venture into the mecha genre.

The story is set on a future Earth where natural resources have been depleted and humanity looks to the tenth planet, Promete, for the first exploration team is destroyed survival. When by betrayal, a megalomaniac named Mr. Doppler emerges, building a vast military force to claim Promete for himself. Earth's governments begin constructing massive combat robots to oppose him, but Doppler destroys them all—except for Danguard Ace. The series follows Takuma Ichimonji, son of the man who led the doomed Promete expedition, who joins Danguard's base as a cadet hoping to restore his father's honor.

entries.title: War of the Planets
entries.creator: Antonio Margheriti
entries.pitch:
War of the Planets is a 1966 Italian sci-fi adventure and the second entry in Antonio Margheriti's Gamma-One series. In the late 21st century, humanity has expanded into space, with colonies on the Moon and Mars. When astronauts on routine patrol encounter mysterious alien vessels, they trigger an interstellar conflict that threatens to consume Earth.

The film blends pulp sci-fi excitement with Cold War anxiety, reflecting 1960s fears of technological infiltration. The aliens—tall, silent beings with telepathic powers—prove far more sophisticated than humanity's military might. Margheriti delivers spectacular set pieces: space battles, alien infiltrators walking among humans, and a dramatic showdown above the Earth. The tone is earnest adventure, played straight without the camp that would characterize later entries in the series.

For fans of Italian genre cinema, this represents Margheriti at his most ambitious before declining into cheaper productions. The production values exceed typical European sci-fi, with elaborate sets and convincing miniatures. The result is a thrilling artifact of 1960s European science fiction cinema.

entries.title: War with the Newts
entries.creator: Karel Čapek
entries.pitch: War with the Newts is a prescient 1936 satirical science fiction novel by Czech author Karel Čapek, best known for coining the word "robot" in his earlier work R.U.R. In this novel, a seafarer discovers an intelligent race of newts in the Indian Ocean who possess limited but developing intelligence. Initially exploited for pearl farming and manual labor, the newts rapidly acquire human knowledge and technology, eventually rebelling against their human overlords. The story culminates in a global war between humanity and the newt civilization—a darkly comedic exploration of colonialism, nationalism, and the cyclical nature of oppression.

entries.title: Warning from Space
entries.creator: Koji Shima
entries.pitch:
Warning from Space is a 1956 Japanese tokusatsu science fiction film that holds an important place in cinematic history as the nation's first full-colored science fiction film and the first to feature a developed extraterrestrial race. Directed by Koji Shima and produced by Masaichi Nagata at Daiei Film, it emerged in the wake of Godzilla's success, part of a wave of 1950s Japanese monster and sci-fi films exploring atomic-age anxieties.

The film centers on the Pairans, starfish-like aliens from a world on the opposite side of the Sun, who travel to Earth to warn humanity of an imminent collision with a rogue planet dubbed Planet R. To avoid panicking the public, one alien takes human form—disguising herself as popular Japanese entertainer Hikari Aozora. The film's vision of friendly aliens assisting humanity against a cosmic threat, combined with its striking avant-garde alien designs by renowned artist Tarō Okamoto, makes it a fascinating artifact of early Japanese science fiction cinema.

entries.title: Wasteland
entries.creator: Interplay Productions / Electronic Arts
entries.pitch: Wasteland is a pioneering post-apocalyptic role-playing game set in 2087, decades after nuclear war devastated civilization. Players control a team of Desert Rangers, peacekeepers operating in the American Southwest, who investigate disturbances in surrounding areas and discover a sinister plot by an ancient artificial intelligence called Base Cochise. The game features strategic turn-based combat, character progression, and a non-linear world that responds to player actions—establishing many conventions that would later define the RPG genre and directly inspiring the Fallout series.

entries.title: Wave Without a Shore
entries.creator: C.J. Cherryh
entries.pitch: Wave Without a Shore is a 1981 science fiction novel by C.J. Cherryh, published by DAW Books as part of her Alliance-Union universe. The novel explores what happens when humans encounter an alien reality that operates on fundamentally different perceptual and existential principles. The story follows a human who finds himself stranded in a reality where the laws of physics and perception work differently, forcing him to adapt to survive. Cherryh, known for her rigorous approach to hard science fiction and complex alien psychology, uses this novella-length work as a thought experiment in how humans might cope with truly alien environments—ones that challenge not just their bodies but their very conception of reality. Originally published alongside Port Eternity and Voyager in Night as part of Cherryh's "magic cookie" books, this novel represents her exploration of themes of identity, perception, and what it means to be human when confronted with the truly unknown.

entries.title: We
entries.creator: Yevgeny Zamyatin
entries.pitch: We is a dystopian novel written in 1920-1921 by Russian writer Yevgeny Zamyatin, depicting a future society of absolute conformity and totalitarian control. The story follows D-503, a spacecraft engineer living in the One State, a glass-walled civilization where citizens are identified by numbers rather than names, and where all aspects of life are governed by strict mathematical logic and the will of the mysterious Benefactor. When D-503 begins to experience forbidden emotions and develops a sense of individuality, he must confront the foundations of his society—and his own humanity.

entries.title: We
entries.creator: Vojtěch Jasný
entries.pitch:
In a world of perfect conformity, one man begins to question everything. Based on Yevgeny Zamyatin's prophetic 1921 novel—the work that inspired George Orwell's 1984 and Aldous Huxley's Brave New World—We presents a chilling vision of a totalitarian state built on mathematical precision and rational efficiency.

One thousand years after the One State's conquest of the world, the massive spaceship Integral is under construction, designed to spread the state's proven recipe for justice and happiness to other planets. Its chief engineer, D-503 (Dieter Laser), is a model citizen—until he meets I-330 (Sabine von Maydell), a woman whose very existence is an act of rebellion. Against the backdrop of glass walls and uniformed citizens marching in perfect step, D-503 begins to experience something the state cannot tolerate: the stirrings of individual thought and forbidden emotion.

The film is a meditation on the price of perfection—and the indomitable human spirit that resists it.

entries.title: We Called Him Robert
entries.creator: Ilya Olshvanger
entries.pitch: A Soviet scientist creates a humanoid robot named Robert, designed as his exact duplicate to explore space too dangerous for humans. When Robert is sent into human society on a date, he unexpectedly \"falls in love\" and begins to develop genuine emotions — becoming more human than his rationalistic creator ever intended. This 1967 Soviet science fiction comedy explores the boundary between machine and man with gentle humor and surprising emotional depth.

entries.title: Weathering With You
entries.creator: Makoto Shinkai
entries.pitch: Weathering With You is a visually stunning 2019 Japanese animated romantic fantasy film directed by Makoto Shinkai, the creator of the global phenomenon Your Name. The story follows 16-year-old Hodaka Morishima, who runs away from his troubled rural home to rain-soaked Tokyo, where he befriends Hina Amano, an orphaned girl with the miraculous ability to control the weather. Together, they launch an underground business offering to clear the sky for special events, bringing brief moments of sunshine to a city drowning in endless rain. As their business gains popularity, Hina's powers begin taking a devastating physical toll—her body slowly turns to water with each use. The film explores themes of youthful rebellion, socioeconomic hardship, and the choice between personal happiness and saving the world.

entries.title: Welcome II the Terrordome
entries.creator: Ngozi Onwurah
entries.pitch:
Welcome II the Terrordome is a bold 1995 British sci-fi film that presents a brutal dystopian vision of a future where Black people have been forcibly segregated into a massive inner-city ghetto called the Terrordome. Directed by Ngozi Onwurah, one of Britain's few Black female filmmakers of the era, this film serves as a sharp allegory for colonialism, racism, and the structural violence of systemic oppression.

The story follows Spike and his sister Anjela, who live trapped within the Terrordome's walls. When Spike's pregnant white girlfriend Jodie seeks refuge there after fleeing an abusive relationship, the tensions of race, class, and power explode. After a police trap results in the death of Spike's young nephew Hector, Anjela embarks on a violent rampage against the police.

Onwurah's film is notable for its unapologetic engagement with issues of race, gender, and power. The Terrordome itself is a powerful visual metaphor for the racialized ghettos created by decades of discriminatory housing policy and social neglect. The film was controversial upon release for its explicit violence and unflinching critique of both institutional racism and internal community tensions.

entries.title: Welcome to the Space Show
entries.creator: Koji Masunari (Director), Hideyuki Kurata (Writer)
entries.pitch: Welcome to the Space Show is a 2010 Japanese animated science fiction film produced by A-1 Pictures and distributed by Aniplex. Directed by Koji Masunari from a script by Hideyuki Kurata, the film tells the story of five elementary school children who rescue an alien dog and are rewarded with a trip to the Moon. When circumstances leave them stranded in space, they must journey across the galaxy to return home before their parents arrive for the school trip. The film was described by its producers as surpassing Star Wars in scale, and premiered at the 60th Berlin International Film Festival in February 2010.

entries.title: Weltraumschiff 1 startet...
entries.creator: Anton Kutter
entries.pitch:
Weltraumschiff 1 startet... (Spaceship Number 1 Starts) is a remarkable German short film from 1940, directed by Anton Kutter. This pioneering science fiction short depicts the first manned flight to the Moon, chronicling Spaceship-1's historic journey commanded by Commodore Hardt, the inventor of a powerful rocket fuel called "Neotan-X." 

Produced during a remarkable period in German cinema history, the film combines scientific enthusiasm with narrative storytelling, presenting a vision of space exploration that was decades ahead of its time. The production involved filming before television crews and thousands of spectators at the actual launch event, adding an unprecedented documentary quality to this fictional narrative.

entries.title: When Gravity Fails
entries.pitch:
In the late 22nd century, the world has been turned upside down. The Islamic Middle East has risen to global dominance while the once-mighty West—America, Europe, the Soviet Union—has fractured into petty squabbling states, their citizens now naively touring the ascendant Arab world like wide-eyed pilgrims. In the neon-drenched Budayeen, the notorious entertainment and criminal district of an unnamed Levantine city, small-time hustler Marîd Audran ekes out a precarious living through charm, wits, and heavy drug use.

What makes Audran remarkable in this wired world is his Luddite fear of neural modification—most citizens have their brains "wired" with add-ons ("daddies") that grant skills or whole personalities ("moddies") on demand. Audran refuses this augmentation, relying instead on his street smarts and excessive stimulants. But when a brutal serial killer begins murdering people in the Budayeen, Audran is thrust into an investigation that will force him to confront his deepest fears—literally—by submitting to the very cybernetic modifications he despises.

This is cyberpunk with a twist: a reversal of the genre's typical Western-centric future, grounded in Middle Eastern culture and a deeply flawed, sympathetic protagonist whose journey into technological transformation mirrors his psychological transformation.

entries.title: When It Changed
entries.creator: Joanna Russ
entries.pitch: On the far-off planet Whileaway, a plague wiped out men centuries ago, leaving women to build a peaceful, rational society free from the hierarchies and violence of the old world. When a ship from Earth finally arrives—carrying men who want to "resettle" the planet and reclaim it for humanity—the women of Whileaway face an existential choice. This Nebula Award-winning short story is a sharp, subversive examination of gender, power, and what "civilization" truly means. Joanna Russ writes with incisive wit and fierce intelligence, turning the conventions of space colonization science fiction inside out.

entries.title: White Hole
entries.creator: Toshio Matsumoto
entries.pitch:
White Hole is a mesmerizing six-minute experimental journey through the psychedelic vastness of space, directed by avant-garde filmmaker Toshio Matsumoto. Created in 1979, this short film represents a unique fusion of visual art and science fiction cinema—a brief but profound meditation on the cosmos and human consciousness.

The film presents an abstract, dreamlike exploration of space imagery, where visual compositions seem to emerge from and dissolve back into the cosmic void. Working with composer Joji Yuasa's electronic score, Matsumoto creates an immersive audiovisual experience that feels less like a narrative film and more like a portal into another dimension. The white hole of the title suggests both an absence and a presence—a gateway or transformation point in the fabric of space-time.

For fans of experimental cinema and psychedelic art films, White Hole offers a rare glimpse into the Japanese avant-garde scene of the late 1970s, when artists were exploring consciousness through the lens of Eastern philosophy and cosmic wonder.

entries.title: White Plastic Sky
entries.creator: Katalin Tóth
entries.pitch:
In 2123, humanity faces extinction through resource depletion. The solution is radical: at age 50, every citizen voluntarily transforms into a tree, becoming part of a growing forest that produces oxygen and restores the planet. This is not death — it is transcendence into nature.

When Stefan discovers that his beloved wife Nora has secretly signed up to become a tree before her time, he is devastated. The system is already consuming her — she fades more each day, her skin taking on the texture of bark. Desperate to save her, Stefan embarks on an adventurous journey through a world transformed by millions of human-turned-trees, racing against the clock before she completes her transformation.

White Plastic Sky is a haunting meditation on mortality, love, and what it means to leave a legacy. The animation is gorgeous — trees grow from human forms, their branches reaching toward a plastic-gray sky, their faces frozen in expressions of peace or terror. The film asks: if you could become part of the solution, would you? And what if love made you refuse?

entries.title: Who Wants to Kill Jessie?
entries.creator: Václav Vorlíček (director), Miloš Macourek (writer)
entries.pitch: Who Wants to Kill Jessie? is a 1966 Czechoslovak science fiction comedy that explores what happens when dreams become reality. The film follows a married couple of scientists—doc. Růženka Beránková and doc. Jindřich Beránek—who invent a machine that can materialize objects and characters from dreams into the real world. Their goal is relatively modest: to help patients express their subconscious desires through art. But when Beránek's dream of the perfect American woman Jessie is accidentally brought to life, chaos ensues. The film is notable for its innovative visual effects, including actual comic book panels appearing in live-action scenes, and for its sly commentary on the clash between socialist realism and Western popular culture.

entries.title: Wicked City
entries.creator: Yoshiaki Kawajiri (Director), Based on "Wicked City: Black Guard" by Hideyuki Kikuchi
entries.pitch: Wicked City is a 1987 Japanese adult animated neo-noir action film that explores the hidden boundary between the human world and the "Black World" — an alternate dimension populated by supernatural demons. The story follows Renzaburō Taki, a Black Guard agent who protects the treaty between humans and demons, partnered with Makie, a beautiful demon woman. Together, they must protect a 200-year-old mystic who signs a crucial peace treaty, while battling radical demons who seek to destroy the fragile harmony between worlds. Directed by Yoshiaki Kawajiri (who would later direct Ninja Scroll), this is a stylish, violent, and sexually charged supernatural action film that predates the cyberpunk boom.

entries.title: Wielka, większa i największa
entries.creator: Jerzy Broszkiewicz
entries.pitch:
Wielka, większa i największa (Great, Greater, and Greatest) is a Polish science fiction young adult novel by Jerzy Broszkiewicz, published in 1960 by Nasza Księgarnia. The story follows two exceptionally intelligent teenagers—Ika and Groszek—who embark on three increasingly ambitious adventures guided by a mysterious talking Opel Kapitän car. Their first adventure involves rescuing a kidnapped child, the second sees them locating survivors of a plane crash in the Sahara, and the third takes them across the galaxy to defend humanity before alien beings from the Vega star system.

Originally published in the "Klub Siedmiu Przygód" (Club of Seven Adventures) series, the novel became required reading in Polish schools from 1970 and was included on the Special Hans Christian Andersen Honor List in 1979. The book was adapted into a film in 1963, directed by Anna Sokołowska, and has been translated into multiple languages including Czech, Russian, German, and Hungarian.

entries.title: Wing Commander
entries.creator: Chris Roberts, Origin Systems
entries.pitch: Wing Commander is the seminal space combat simulation that defined a genre and brought the epic scale of Star Wars-style space warfare to personal computers. Released in 1990 by Origin Systems, this groundbreaking game placed players in the cockpit of a fighter spacecraft during an interstellar war between humanity's Terran Confederation and the predatory Kilrathi alien empire. What set Wing Commander apart was its combination of cinematic presentation, branching narrative, and accessible flight mechanics—creating an experience that felt like controlling your own science fiction film. The game was considered a major leap forward for space combat games, featuring graphics, audio, and a story campaign that invited comparison to the Star Wars films. It spawned one of the most successful franchises in gaming history and established many conventions that would define space combat games for decades to come.

entries.title: Wizards
entries.creator: Ralph Bakshi
entries.pitch: In a world devastated by nuclear war, two twin wizards are born—one representing the forces of magic, the other technology. This post-apocalyptic animated epic follows Avatar, the kind-hearted fairy wizard, as he must stop his evil brother Blackwolf from unleashing ancient propaganda technology to conquer the last peaceful kingdom. It's a psychedelic blend of fantasy, science fiction, and political allegory that predates many modern animated films.

entries.title: Wolf's Hole
entries.creator: Věra Chytilová
entries.pitch: Wolf's Hole is a 1986 Czechoslovak science fiction horror film directed by the acclaimed Věra Chytilová, best known for her landmark Czech New Wave work Daisies. The film follows a group of teenagers who are invited to a remote skiing workshop in the mountains, but things quickly take a sinister turn when the supervisors reveal there should only be ten participants—not eleven. As the group is cut off from the outside world, the supervisors begin turning the teenagers against each other, creating an atmosphere of paranoia and hostility. The teens eventually discover their captors are extraterrestrials demanding a sacrifice. The film was entered into the 37th Berlin International Film Festival and nominated for the Golden Bear for Best Film.

entries.title: Woman in the Moon
entries.creator: Fritz Lang (director), Thea von Harbou (screenplay)
entries.pitch: Woman in the Moon (Frau im Mond) is a groundbreaking German silent science fiction film directed by Fritz Lang, considered one of the first "serious" science fiction films ever made. Released in 1929, it presented the basics of rocket travel to a mass audience for the first time, including the revolutionary use of a multi-stage rocket design. The film tells the story of an entrepreneur named Helius who finances a rocket expedition to the Moon after learning from Professor Mannfeldt that the Moon may contain vast deposits of gold. Alongside a crew including his assistant Friede, the professor, and other team members, Helius embarks on what becomes a perilous journey to the Moon's far side, where they discover a breathable atmosphere and confirm the presence of gold—but also face a deadly crisis when their oxygen supplies run low and one person must make the ultimate sacrifice.

entries.title: World of Tomorrow
entries.creator: Don Hertzfeldt
entries.pitch:
World of Tomorrow is a series of animated science fiction short films written, directed, produced, animated, and edited by Don Hertzfeldt. The series began with Episode One in 2015, followed by Episode Two in 2017 and Episode Three in 2020. The first film was nominated for Best Animated Short Film at the 2015 Academy Awards. All three films feature the voice of Julia Pott alongside Hertzfeldt's four-year-old niece Winona Mae, whose spontaneous reactions were recorded and edited into the stories to create her character Emily Prime.

The series follows a young girl named Emily who is contacted by a third-generation clone of her future self from 227 years in the future, created as a means of achieving immortality. The clone explains the myriad ways people in her time have sought to escape death and loneliness through technology. The design of the film was influenced by science fiction novels and magazine covers of the 1950s and '60s, with Hertzfeldt wanting a storybook aesthetic.

entries.title: World on a Wire
entries.creator: Rainer Werner Fassbinder (Director), based on the novel "Simulacron-3" by Daniel F. Galouye
entries.pitch: World on a Wire is a haunting German television miniseries that explores the nature of reality through the story of a researcher at the Institute for Cybernetics and Futurology. When identity units begin vanishing and memories start glitching in a simulated world, investigator Stiller discovers a disturbing truth: the "real" world he inhabits may itself be just another layer of simulation. Fassbinder crafts a slow-burning, intellectually dense thriller that prioritizes philosophical questions over action, creating a bleak meditation on identity, consciousness, and the nature of existence itself. This is simulation theory decades before The Matrix made it mainstream.

entries.title: Xenon
entries.creator: Masaomi Kanzaki
entries.pitch: Xenon (also known as Heavy Metal Warrior Xenon) is a Japanese manga series created by Masaomi Kanzaki, serialized in Shogakukan's Shōnen Big Comic from 1986 to 1987 before being abruptly canceled. The story follows a young man named Asuka who wakes up in contemporary Japan with no memory of his past, wandering alone and confused through the city. He soon discovers the horrifying truth: he is the product of a clandestine experiment conducted by a mysterious organization. When he gets angry, he transforms into a powerful android—a super-cyborg designed as part of a covert corporate weapon research program. With his newfound powers, Asuka embarks on a mission of revenge against those who turned him into a living weapon. The series was collected into four tankōbon volumes and gained a sequel titled Xenon: 199X R in 2006.

entries.title: Yokohama Kaidashi Kikou
entries.creator: Hitoshi Ashinano (Manga), Takashi Annō/Tomomi Mochizuki (OVA Direction)
entries.pitch:
In a quiet, post-apocalyptic Japan where humanity is slowly declining after environmental collapse, an android named Alpha Hatsuseno runs a small coffee shop called Café Alpha on the lonely coast of the Miura Peninsula. Unlike the humans around her who age and eventually die, Alpha is immortal—a prototype robot who was left behind by her owner on an indefinite journey. Through episodic, slice-of-life stories, the series follows Alpha's daily activities: brewing coffee, taking photographs on her scooter, befriending the locals, and encountering other robots and mysterious phenomena in this gently decaying world.

What makes Yokohama Kaidashi Kikou extraordinary is its tone—a contemplative, meditative approach to the end of human civilization. Rather than dystopian despair, the series offers a gentle acceptance of mortality and change, filled with what the Japanese call "mono no aware" (the bittersweet awareness of impermanence). The OVA adaptations beautifully capture this atmosphere with sparse dialogue, lush environmental detail, and a profound sense of time passing.

entries.title: Yongary, Monster from the Deep
entries.creator: Kim Ki-duk (Director)
entries.pitch:
Yongary, Monster from the Deep is a landmark 1967 South Korean kaiju film that stands as one of the earliest examples of Korean science fiction cinema. Directed by Kim Ki-duk (no relation to the later controversial filmmaker of the same name), this joint South Korean-Japanese production was created to capitalize on the success of Toho's Godzilla series and features the same practical effects techniques—suitmation, pyrotechnics, and miniature sets—that defined Japanese monster movies of the era.

Set in contemporary Seoul, the film follows a giant reptilian monster that emerges from beneath the Earth after a nuclear test in the Middle East triggers an earthquake on the Korean Peninsula. As Yongary rampages toward Seoul, the military struggles to contain the creature while a young scientist races to find a chemical weakness that might stop the destruction. The film is notable for its ambitious production values for the time, including elaborate miniature city sets and a detailed monster suit constructed in Japan under the supervision of Masao Yagi, who previously built suits for the Gamera series.

Despite being considered a lost film in Korea for over four decades—until a damaged 48-minute print was recovered by the Korean Film Archive—Yongary has achieved cult status internationally and was featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000. The film represents a fascinating artifact of Cold War anxieties filtered through a distinctly Korean lens, blending Japanese tokusatsu techniques with Korean storytelling.

entries.title: You Are Empty
entries.creator: Mandel ArtPlains, Digital Spray Studios
entries.pitch: You Are Empty is a first-person shooter set in an alternate-history Soviet Union in 1955. The player wakes up in a ruined hospital to discover that a massive government experiment to create "super-humans" has catastrophically failed, leaving most of the population dead or transformed into homicidal mutants. As a mid-ranking military officer, the player must fight through the desolate wasteland of the Soviet Union, unravel the mystery behind the disaster, and survive encounters with both mutant survivors and hostile Soviet military units. Developed by Ukrainian studios Mandel ArtPlains and Digital Spray Studios, the game combines atmospheric exploration with period-accurate Soviet aesthetics to create a uniquely haunting post-apocalyptic experience.

entries.title: You Are a Widow, Sir
entries.creator: Václav Vorlíček
entries.pitch: You Are a Widow, Sir (Pane, vy jste vdova!) is a 1970 Czechoslovak comedy science fiction film directed by Václav Vorlíček. In the near future, King Rosebud IV of a fictional European kingdom decides to disband his army after an accident injures his cousin. The army generals, fearing for their positions, plot to assassinate the king using an elaborate scheme involving a brain transplant—implanting the mind of a convicted murderess into a synthetic duplicate of a famous actress.

entries.title: Z.P.G.
entries.creator: Michael Campus (Director)
entries.pitch: Z.P.G. (Zero Population Growth) is a 1972 British-American dystopian science fiction film directed by Michael Campus, starring Oliver Reed and Geraldine Chaplin. Set in a severely overpopulated and polluted future Earth, the film explores a world where the global government has decreed a 30-year ban on having children, enforced by the death penalty. Couples who long for children are given animatronic robot substitutes to satisfy their maternal instincts. When a couple secretly conceives a child, they must hide the baby from both the authorities and their jealous neighbors in a terrifying world where simply screaming "baby" brings the police.

entries.title: Zaat
entries.creator: Don Barton
entries.pitch:
Zaat (also known as Blood Waters of Dr. Z) is a 1971 American independent science fiction horror film produced on a shoestring budget of $50,000. The film stars Marshall Grauer as Dr. Kurt Leopold, a mad scientist whose formula for transforming humans into sea creature hybrids is ridiculed by his colleagues. After injecting himself with his serum and transforming into a catfish-like monster, Dr. Leopold seeks revenge on those who scorned him, releasing mutated walking catfish across town and contaminating the water supply.

The film was produced and directed by Don Barton and filmed over one month in 1970 in various Florida locations including Rainbow Springs, Green Cove Springs, and Marineland. Originally distributed by Horizon Films, it found limited theatrical release, earning only $200 on its first showing in Manhattan before being pulled from theaters.

entries.title: Zanox
entries.creator: Márk Gergely Borbás
entries.pitch: In contemporary Budapest, a young man named Misi becomes an unwilling subject in a clandestine medical experiment. The twist: the experimental drug grants him the ability to travel through time—but only if he drinks from a specific homemade spirit. This quirky Hungarian sci-fi comedy blends time travel paradoxes with the absurd logic of dream logic, creating a surreal narrative where the rules of causality bend and twist like the smoke from Misi's magical drink. The film plays like a midnight movie fever dream, mixing low-budget practical effects with genuine emotional stakes.

entries.title: Zardoz
entries.creator: John Boorman
entries.pitch: In a distant 2293, humanity has split into two species: the immortal "Eternals" who live in luxury within a hidden paradise called the Vortex, and the mortal "Brutals" who toil in irradiated wastelands, growing food for their masters. When Zed, a Brutal Exterminator, stows away aboard Zardoz—the flying stone god the Brutals worship—he discovers the terrible truth behind his world: he is the product of a eugenics experiment, engineered to penetrate the Vortex and destroy the stagnant eternal society. What follows is a surreal journey of revelation, revolution, and rebirth.

entries.title: Zarex
entries.creator: Richard Abelardo (Director)
entries.pitch:
Zarex is a 1958 Filipino science fiction film produced by LVN Pictures, making it one of the earliest Filipino science fiction films ever made. Directed by Richard Abelardo, the film tells the story of Filipino astronauts who land on the moon, marking a pioneering moment in Philippine cinema. The film features Willie Sotelo and Carmencita Abad in the lead roles, and showcases the launching of a spaceship and the historic landing of humans on the moon—a remarkable feat for Filipino cinema at a time when such ambitious science fiction productions were rare outside of Hollywood and Japan.

The film was produced during the golden age of Philippine cinema in the 1950s, a period when the country was producing hundreds of films annually and developing its own unique voice in Asian cinema. Zarex represents an ambitious attempt to compete with Hollywood's science fiction offerings like "Destination Moon" (1950), which had won an Academy Award for Best Special Effects. The Filipino production aimed to bring a similar vision of space exploration to local audiences, albeit with the limited resources of the Philippine film industry at the time.

entries.title: Zombies of the Stratosphere
entries.creator: Fred C. Brannon (Director)
entries.pitch: Zombies of the Stratosphere is a 1952 Republic Studios serial film that represents some of the final flowering of the classic science fiction movie serial genre. The film features Larry Martin, a leader in the Inter-Planetary Patrol, who investigates a rocketship landing on Earth and discovers Martian invaders led by a being called Marex. The Martians, whose home planet is dying due to being too far from the Sun, plan to use stolen hydrogen bomb technology to shift Earth's orbit and swap positions with Mars—effectively destroying all life on Earth to save their own civilization. Martin must stop them using his jet-powered flying suit and helmet, battling both the extraterrestrial threat and Earthly criminals hired by the alien renegade scientist Dr. Harding.

entries.title: Zoo zéro
entries.creator: Alain Fleischer
entries.pitch:
Set in a surreal nightclub called Noah's Ark where guests wear animal masks, Zoo zéro follows Eva, a singer who seeks to evade the control of her agent by wandering the city at night. The film features Klaus Kinski in a supporting role as the mysterious figure Yavé, who observes the action from the margins.

This experimental French film from 1979 creates a dreamlike atmosphere where reality and fantasy blur. The nightclub sequences show performers and patrons in elaborate animal costumes, creating a grotesque carnival aesthetic. Eva moves through both the club and the nocturnal city streets, searching for escape from the forces that constrain her.

entries.title: Zork
entries.creator: Tim Anderson, Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels (Infocom)
entries.pitch: Zork is a groundbreaking text adventure game released in 1977, developed by a team of MIT students who would go on to found Infocom. Widely considered the most famous interactive fiction ever created, Zork placed players in the role of an explorer navigating the abandoned Great Underground Empire—a vast underground world filled with treasure, puzzles, and danger. Players typed commands in natural language to move through hundreds of locations, interact with objects, and solve intricate puzzles. The game's sophisticated parser could understand complex sentences far beyond the simple two-word commands of earlier text adventures, creating an unprecedented sense of immersion. Zork was included in the Library of Congress's game canon in 2007 as one of the ten most important video games in history.
